rulesUlster.point: an chopail, abairt rangaithe (Is + ainmfhocal + é/í)
rulesUlster.statement: To say what a person is, the copula Is comes first, then the noun, then the pronoun: Is dochtúir é, Is múinteoir í. The pronoun é or í matches the sex of the person named.

rulesUlster.point: an chopail, ceist agus freagra (An ... é? Is ea / Ní hea)
rulesUlster.statement: A classification question is formed with An + noun + é/í? and is answered with Is ea or Ní hea, never with tá. A correction can be added with atá ann: Ní hea. Dochtúir atá ann. (In Ulster speech Is ea is often heard as 'Sea; pupils write Is ea.)

rulesUlster.point: an chopail, Cén tslí bheatha atá ag ...?
rulesUlster.statement: A person's occupation is asked with Cad é an tslí bheatha atá ag X? or Cad é an obair atá aige/aici? and answered with a copula sentence: Is polaiteoir é. The standard Cén tslí bheatha / Cén obair is also understood.

rulesUlster.point: an chopail i gclásal indíreach (gur)
rulesUlster.statement: After a verb of opinion such as sílim, ceapaim or measaim, the copula Is becomes gur: Sílim gur feirmeoir é. Sílim is the usual Ulster verb; ceapaim and measaim are also correct.

rulesUlster.point: an chopail leis an aidiacht, Nach ... an ... é?
rulesUlster.statement: An adjective can be placed before the noun with the copula for emphasis: Nach deas an rothar é? The answer repeats only the copula and the adjective: Is deas.

rulesUlster.point: an chopail san aimsir chaite, Ba / B'
rulesUlster.statement: In the past tense the copula is Ba, which lenites the adjective after it, and B' before a vowel: Ba chumasach an cainteoir é, B'uafásach an timpiste í. Adjectives beginning with l, n, r or sp do not change in writing: Ba leadránach, Ba spórtúil.

rulesUlster.point: inscne agus an forainm é/í
rulesUlster.statement: With a feminine noun the pronoun at the end is í (aimsir, áit, ceist, fadhb, obair, timpiste); with a masculine noun it is é. The book marks feminine nouns with í in the exercise stems.

rulesUlster.point: Sin é / Sin í / Sin iad
rulesUlster.statement: To point someone out, Sin is followed by é, í or iad and then the name: Sin í Niamh, Sin é Peadar, Sin iad na cailíní.

rulesUlster.point: is maith le, is breá le, is fuath le
rulesUlster.statement: Liking and disliking are expressed with the copula and the preposition le: Is maith le Peadar peil, Is fuath le Séamas deoch leighis. With a pronoun, le combines into liom, leat, leis, léi, linn, libh, leo.

rulesUlster.point: freagra ar An maith leat ...?
rulesUlster.statement: A question with An maith leat? is answered by repeating the copula: Is maith liom, Is aoibhinn liom, Is breá liom for a positive reply, or Ní maith liom, Is fuath liom, Is gráin liom for a negative one. The negative of Is is Ní.

rulesUlster.point: is fearr le, rogha idir dhá rud
rulesUlster.statement: Preference uses is fearr le: Cé acu is fearr leat popcheol nó snagcheol? Is fearr liom popcheol. A preference within a category is asked with Cad é an + noun + is fearr leat? and answered Is fearr liom .... The standard Cén + noun + is fearr leat? is also understood.

rulesUlster.point: úinéireacht, Cé leis é? Is liomsa é
rulesUlster.statement: Ownership is expressed with le and the emphatic pronoun: Cé leis an peann? Is liomsa é, Ní liomsa é, An leatsa é? With a name the indirect form is used after sílim or ceapaim: sílim gur le Pól é.

rulesUlster.point: náisiúntacht leis an chopail
rulesUlster.statement: Nationality is a classification sentence of the same shape as occupation: Is Rúiseach é.

paradigmsUlster.title: Is + slí bheatha + é/í
Ceist / Freagra (An ... é?)
forms: An múinteoir é? : Is ea / Ní hea
An rinceoir í? : Is ea / Ní hea
An fiaclóir é? : Ní hea. Dochtúir atá ann.

paradigmsUlster.title: Ceist / Freagra (gur)
forms: Cad é an obair atá aige? : Sílim gur feirmeoir é
Cad é an obair atá aige? : Ceapaim gur feirmeoir é
Cad é an obair atá aige? : Measaim gur feirmeoir é

paradigmsUlster.title: le + forainmneacha
Freagraí ar An maith leat ...?
forms: An maith leat popcheol? : (i) Is maith liom
An maith leat an t-amhrán sin? : (ii) Is maith liom / Is aoibhinn liom / Is breá liom
An maith leat tae milis? : (iii) Ní maith liom / Is fuath liom / Is gráin liom

paradigmsUlster.title: Cé leis? (úinéireacht)
forms: Cé leis an peann? : Is liomsa é
An leatsa é? : Ní liomsa é
Cé leis é? : Níl a fhios agam ach sílim gur le Pól é.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite, an chéad réimniú: séimhiú ar an gconsan tosaigh
rulesUlster.statement: To form the past tense of a first-conjugation verb beginning with a consonant, lenite the initial consonant of the root (the order form): Dún becomes Dhún sé, Cuir becomes Chuir sé, Múch becomes Mhúch sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite: briathra nach nglacann séimhiú (l, n, r, sc, sp, st)
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs whose root begins with a letter or cluster that cannot take lenition keep the root unchanged in the past tense: Las sé an tine, Scuab sé an t-úrlár, Rith sé go dtí an líne.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite: ceist agus diúltach le Ar agus Níor
rulesUlster.statement: The question is formed with Ar and the negative with Níor, both followed by lenition of the verb: Ar dhún tú? Níor dhún mé. Ar chuir sé? Níor chuir sé. The pronoun subject follows the verb.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite: an chéad phearsa iolra, foirm tháite -amar/-eamar
rulesUlster.statement: In Ulster the first person plural of the past tense is the root (lenited or with d' as usual) followed by the pronoun muid: dhún muid, chuir muid, d'ól muid, d'úsáid muid, d'fhág muid. Question and negative follow the same pattern: Ar dhún muid? Níor dhún muid. The standard synthetic endings -amar and -eamar (dhúnamar, chuireamar) will be met in books and exam papers and should be recognised, but pupils write the muid form.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite: an saorbhriathar, -adh/-eadh
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form adds -adh to a broad root and -eadh to a slender root, and it is never lenited, even after Ar and Níor: Dúnadh, Ar dúnadh? Níor dúnadh; Cuireadh, Ar cuireadh? Níor cuireadh.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite: briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta, d' roimh an mbriathar
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with a vowel takes the prefix d' in the positive past: D'ól sé, D'amharc sé, D'íoc sé, D'úsáid sé, D'éist sé. After Ar and Níor the d' is dropped: Ar ól tú? Níor ól mé. The autonomous form has no d': Óladh, Ar óladh? Níor óladh; Úsáideadh, Níor úsáideadh.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite: briathra a thosaíonn ar 'f', d'fh
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with f is lenited and also takes d' in the positive past: D'fhág sé, D'fhan sé, D'fhill sé, D'fhéach sé. After Ar and Níor there is lenition but no d': Ar fhág tú? Níor fhág mé. The autonomous form is neither lenited nor given d': Fágadh, Ar fágadh? Níor fágadh. Note that for 'look at' Ulster normally says amharc ar (d'amharc sé), so féach appears here only to show the f pattern.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ordú agus an aimsir chaite: an fhréamh chéanna
rulesUlster.statement: The book presents the order (imperative, second person singular) as the root of the verb and derives the past tense directly from it, so Dún an doras gives Dhún sé an doras; a second person possessive in the order becomes third person when reported: Cíor do chuid gruaige gives Chíor sé a chuid gruaige, Sín amach do lámh gives Shín sé amach a lámh.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an chéad réimniú, briathra leathana
rulesUlster.statement: For a first-conjugation verb with a broad final consonant, the present tense is formed by adding -ann to the root, which is the same as the order form: dún gives dúnann sé, glan gives glanann sé, múch gives múchann sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an chéad réimniú, briathra caola
rulesUlster.statement: For a first-conjugation verb with a slender final consonant, -eann is added to the root: cuir gives cuireann sé, blais gives blaiseann sé, rith gives ritheann sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, foirmeacha táite (mé, muid)
rulesUlster.statement: The first person singular has its own ending, -aim after a broad root and -im after a slender one (dúnaim, cuirim). In Ulster the first person plural uses the ordinary -ann/-eann ending followed by muid: dúnann muid, cuireann muid (the book's dúnaimid, cuirimid will be met in printed standard Irish but the app does not ask pupils to write them). All other persons take -ann/-eann followed by the pronoun (dúnann tú, sé, sí, sibh, siad).

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an cheist agus an diúltach
rulesUlster.statement: A question is formed with An followed by eclipsis of the verb (An ndúnann tú? An gcuireann sé?). The negative is formed with Ní followed by lenition (Ní dhúnaim, Ní chuireann sé).

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The free (autonomous) form ends in -tar after a broad root and -tear after a slender root: dúntar, cuirtear. The question is An ndúntar? and the negative Ní dhúntar; the free form has no separate pronoun.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with a vowel takes the same endings (ólann sé, ólaim, ólann muid, óltar) but shows no change after An or Ní because a vowel can be neither eclipsed nor lenited: An ólann tú? Ní ólaim. Longer slender roots such as úsáid and éist follow the same pattern: úsáideann sé, úsáidim, úsáideann muid, úsáidtear, éisteann sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, briathra a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with f is eclipsed to bhf after An (An bhfágann tú?) and lenited to fh after Ní (Ní fhágaim, Ní fhágtar); otherwise it follows the ordinary pattern: fágann sé, fágaim, fágann muid, fágtar.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, úsáid: gnáthghníomh
rulesUlster.statement: The present tense is used for habitual or repeated action, which is why the exercise sentences carry markers such as gach lá, gach oíche, gach tráthnóna, go minic and nuair a bhíonn sé fuar.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, freagra gairid
rulesUlster.statement: A present-tense question is answered by repeating the verb in the right person, positively or negatively, without yes or no: An ndúnann tú an doras? Dúnaim / Ní dhúnaim. An ndúnann sibh an doras? Dúnann muid / Ní dhúnann muid. An ndúntar? Dúntar / Ní dhúntar.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an chéad réimniú, briathra leathana
rulesUlster.statement: To form the future of a broad first conjugation verb, add -faidh to the root: Dún gives Dúnfaidh sé an doras, Glan gives Glanfaidh sé an bord. The book presents this as the answer to an order: the order gives the root, the future says what he will do (Cad é a dhéanfaidh sé?).

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an chéad réimniú, briathra caola
rulesUlster.statement: To form the future of a slender first conjugation verb, add -fidh to the root: Cuir gives Cuirfidh sé an pláta ar an bhord, Bain gives Bainfidh sé an féar. Note the Ulster lenition after ar an: ar an bhord, not ar an mbord.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, ceist agus freagra
rulesUlster.statement: A question is made with An and eclipsis (An ndúnfaidh tú? An gcuirfidh sé?). The answer repeats the verb alone, with the pronoun: Dúnfaidh mé, or in the negative Ní with lenition: Ní dhúnfaidh mé, Ní chuirfidh sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an chéad phearsa iolra
rulesUlster.statement: A question put to sibh is answered in the first person plural. In Ulster the answer is analytic, verb plus muid: Dúnfaidh muid / Ní dhúnfaidh muid, Cuirfidh muid / Ní chuirfidh muid. The book's synthetic forms Dúnfaimid / Ní dhúnfaimid, Cuirfimid / Ní chuirfimid are the standard and pupils will meet them in print.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form of the future is root plus -far (broad) or -fear (slender): Dúnfar an doras, Cuirfear an pláta ar an bhord. Question An ndúnfar? An gcuirfear? Negative Ní dhúnfar, Ní chuirfear.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with a vowel takes no prefix in the future, in the question or in the negative: Ólfaidh sé an deoch, An ólfaidh tú? Ólfaidh mé / Ní ólfaidh mé, An ólfar? Ólfar / Ní ólfar. The same holds for Úsáid, Éist, Íoc and Amharc (the usual Ulster verb for look at).

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, briathra a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with f is eclipsed after An in the question (An bhfágfaidh tú? An bhfágfar?) and lenited after Ní in the negative (Ní fhágfaidh mé, Ní fhágfar). The positive answer has no prefix: Fágfaidh mé. The book's third example, Féach ar an chlár dubh, is kept in the paradigm as an f-verb example only; the everyday Ulster verb for look at is amharc ar, which begins with a vowel and so does not show this point.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an chéad réimniú (achoimre)
rulesUlster.statement: The summary table gives the present: Dúnaim, Dúnann tú, Dúnann sé/sí, Dúnann muid (the book: Dúnaimid), Dúnann sibh, Dúnann siad, autonomous Dúntar (slender Cuirtear), negative Ní dhúnaim, question An ndúnann tú? Verbs in a vowel or f take no prefix in the positive; f is lenited after Ní and eclipsed after An (Ní fhágaim, An bhfágann tú?). The first person singular stays synthetic in Ulster: Dúnaim, Cuirim. In the Fág table the book prints the negative as Ní fhágann, a slip; the paradigm gives Ní fhágaim.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite, an chéad réimniú (achoimre)
rulesUlster.statement: The summary table gives the past: the root is lenited (Dhún mé, Chuir mé) and takes D' before a vowel or f (D'ól mé, D'úsáid mé, D'fhág mé). The first person plural in Ulster is Dhún muid, Chuir muid, D'ól muid, D'úsáid muid, D'fhág muid (the book: Dhúnamar, Chuireamar, D'ólamar, D'úsáideamar, D'fhágamar). Autonomous Dúnadh, Cuireadh, Óladh, Úsáideadh, Fágadh. Negative Níor dhún mé, question Ar dhún tú?, both with lenition.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an chéad réimniú (achoimre)
rulesUlster.statement: The summary table gives the full future for Dún, Cuir, Ól, Úsáid and Fág: Dúnfaidh mé, Dúnfaidh tú, Dúnfaidh sé/sí, Dúnfaidh muid (the book: Dúnfaimid), Dúnfaidh sibh, Dúnfaidh siad, autonomous Dúnfar, negative Ní dhúnfaidh mé, question An ndúnfaidh tú? In the Dún table the book prints the first form as Dúnfaidh with mé dropped; the paradigm supplies it.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha agus an aidiacht bhriathartha, briathra leathana
rulesUlster.statement: The book lists the root, the verbal noun and the verbal adjective of the common broad first conjugation verbs without stating a rule. The usual pattern is verbal noun in -adh (glanadh, dúnadh) with many exceptions (fágáil, fanacht, féachaint, tógáil, ól, amharc). The verbal adjective ends in -tha after b, c, g, m, p, r (scuabtha, pioctha, leagtha, cumtha, ceaptha, gearrtha) and in -ta after d, l, n, s and ch (stadta, díolta, glanta, lasta, múchta); bh and mh become -fa (scríofa, lofa, snáfa), and a root ending in t or th simply adds -a (ata, cleachta, nochta, leata, meata). One entry is worth the principal's eye: the book glosses tolg as smash, but the verb more usually means to contract or catch (an illness); the list keeps the book's gloss. Ulster does not differ enough here to matter for a school app.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha agus an aidiacht bhriathartha, briathra caola
rulesUlster.statement: For slender first conjugation verbs the verbal noun is usually in -eadh (briseadh, filleadh) with many exceptions (baint, bualadh, cur, rith, éisteacht, tuiscint). The verbal adjective ends in -the after b, c, g, m, p, r (béicthe, ligthe, scaipthe, tairgthe, tréigthe, rincthe) and in -te after d, l, n, s (druidte, buailte, sínte, briste); a root ending in t simply adds -e (baiste, loite, tite, scoilte), th drops before -te (caite, braite, maite, rite), and a few are irregular: cuir gives curtha, blais gives blasta, goin gives gonta, mair gives martha. One entry needs the principal's eye: the book gives tairgeadh as the verbal noun of tairg, but the usual form is tairiscint; the list keeps the book's reading. Ulster does not differ enough here to matter for a school app.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite, an dara réimniú, briathra leathana (-aigh)
rulesUlster.statement: To put a broad second-conjugation verb (ending in -aigh) into the past tense, lenite the first consonant of the root and leave the ending as it is: brostaigh becomes bhrostaigh sé, ceannaigh becomes cheannaigh sé. The third person singular form is the lenited root with no ending added.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite, an dara réimniú, briathra caola (-igh)
rulesUlster.statement: Slender second-conjugation verbs (ending in -igh) work the same way: lenite the first consonant and keep the root, so bailigh becomes bhailigh sé, mínigh becomes mhínigh sé, dúisigh becomes dhúisigh sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite, ceist agus diúltach: Ar, Níor
rulesUlster.statement: The question is formed with Ar and the negative with Níor, both followed by lenition: Ar cheannaigh tú? Níor cheannaigh mé. The answer to a question is the verb itself, with or without Níor. For sibh the answer in Ulster usage is the analytic form with muid: Cheannaigh muid / Níor cheannaigh muid (the book prints the synthetic Cheannaíomar / Níor cheannaíomar, which pupils should recognise but need not use).

rulesUlster.point: an saorbhriathar, an aimsir chaite, an dara réimniú
rulesUlster.statement: The free form (saorbhriathar) of the past tense is made by dropping -aigh or -igh and adding -aíodh (broad) or -íodh (slender): ceannaíodh, bailíodh. The free form is not lenited after Ar or Níor: Ar ceannaíodh? Níor ceannaíodh; Ar bailíodh? Níor bailíodh.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A second-conjugation verb beginning with a vowel takes d' in front of it in the positive past tense: d'ullmhaigh sé, d'éirigh sé, d'imigh sé. After Ar and Níor the d' is dropped: Ar ullmhaigh tú? Níor ullmhaigh mé. The free form has no d' either: Ullmhaíodh / Níor ullmhaíodh.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir chaite, briathra a thosaíonn ar 'f'
rulesUlster.statement: A second-conjugation verb beginning with f is both lenited and given d' in the positive past: d'fhiosraigh sé, d'fholmhaigh sé. After Ar and Níor the f is lenited but there is no d': Ar fhiosraigh tú? Níor fhiosraigh mé.

rulesUlster.point: an saorbhriathar, briathra a thosaíonn ar 'f'
rulesUlster.statement: The free form of an f-verb keeps the plain f with no lenition and no d': Fiosraíodh an scéal; Níor fiosraíodh. The question is Ar fiosraíodh an scéal?, in line with the rest of the section (the book prints An fiosraíodh, which is a slip; the app uses Ar).

rulesUlster.point: an dara réimniú, an aimsir láithreach: briathra leathana (-aigh)
rulesUlster.statement: A second conjugation verb whose root ends in broad -aigh drops the -aigh and adds -aíonn for sé, sí, siad and muid: ceannaigh becomes ceannaíonn sé, críochnaigh becomes críochnaíonn sé. The first person singular ends in -aím (ceannaím). The first person plural is the analytic form with muid: ceannaíonn muid, críochnaíonn muid (the book prints ceannaímid).

rulesUlster.point: an dara réimniú, an aimsir láithreach: briathra caola (-igh)
rulesUlster.statement: A second conjugation verb whose root ends in slender -igh drops the -igh and adds -íonn: bailigh becomes bailíonn sé, mínigh becomes míníonn sé. The first person singular ends in -ím (bailím). The first person plural is bailíonn muid, míníonn muid (the book prints bailímid).

rulesUlster.point: an cheist agus an diúltach san aimsir láithreach
rulesUlster.statement: A question is formed with An, which eclipses the verb (An gceannaíonn tú? An mbailíonn sí?), and the negative with Ní, which lenites it (Ní cheannaíonn sé, Ní bhailíonn siad). There is no separate word for yes or no; the answer repeats the verb in the right person: Ceannaím / Ní cheannaím.

rulesUlster.point: an freagra: athrú pearsan
rulesUlster.statement: When a question is answered the person changes: a question with tú is answered with the -ím form (An mbailíonn tú? Bailím) and a question with sibh with the muid form (An mbailíonn sibh? Bailíonn muid). Questions with sé, sí and siad keep the same pronoun in the answer.

rulesUlster.point: briathra sa dara réimniú a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with a vowel is written unchanged after both An and Ní in the present tense: An ullmhaíonn tú? Ullmhaím / Ní ullmhaím; An aimsíonn sé? Ní aimsíonn sé. No h or n is prefixed.

rulesUlster.point: briathra sa dara réimniú a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with f takes bhf after An (An bhfiosraíonn tú?) and fh after Ní (Ní fhiosraíonn sé), so the f is silent in both the question and the negative.

rulesUlster.point: an saorbhriathar, an aimsir láithreach
rulesUlster.statement: The free (autonomous) form ends in -aítear for broad verbs and -ítear for slender verbs: ceannaítear, ullmhaítear, bailítear, deisítear na gluaisteáin. It is questioned and negated like the other forms: An gceannaítear? Ceannaítear / Ní cheannaítear; An bhfiosraítear? Ní fhiosraítear.

rulesUlster.point: forainm réamhfhoclach sa fhreagra
rulesUlster.statement: When an order containing a prepositional pronoun is reported, that pronoun agrees with the new subject: the order Imigh leat becomes Imíonn sé leis (and Imíonn sí léi, Imíonn muid linn).

rulesUlster.point: nóta Ultach: an chéad phearsa iolra agus Céard
rulesUlster.statement: Throughout this section the book's synthetic first person plural (ceannaímid, bailímid, ullmhaímid, aimsímid, fiosraímid) is given for the app as ceannaíonn muid, bailíonn muid, ullmhaíonn muid, aimsíonn muid, fiosraíonn muid. The six exercise B stems Éirímid, Fiafraímid, Ceistímid, Smaoinímid, Críochnaímid and Cuardaímid have been drafted as Éiríonn muid, Fiafraíonn muid, Ceistíonn muid, Smaoiníonn muid, Críochnaíonn muid and Cuardaíonn muid, flagged for the principal's decision. The column heading Céard a dhéanann sé? is given as Cad é a dhéanann sé? Where the book has gach lá, gach bliain, gach maidin, the Ulster text has achan lá, achan bhliain, achan mhaidin.

rulesUlster.point: nóta eagarthóireachta: earráidí cló sa leabhar féin
rulesUlster.statement: Five misprints in the book itself (not OCR errors) have been corrected in this extract: the order Corraigh na leite (the answer column has an leite, which is right), the order Ainmigh na daoine sin and its answer Aimníonn sé na daoine (both for Ainmnigh / Ainmníonn), Reitigh twice in exercise C for Réitigh, and Cuardaimid in exercise B for Cuardaímid. Three further fada slips, which may be print or OCR, have also been corrected silently: greithe in both columns of the Triomaigh row (for gréithe), An eiríonn in exercise A items 1 and 2 (for An éiríonn), and on scoil in exercise A item 11 (for ón scoil). In paradigm C the book prints Ullmhaíonn / Ní ullmhaíonn sé with sé missing from the first half of the sé row; the extract supplies it.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an dara réimniú, briathra leathana (-aigh)
rulesUlster.statement: For a broad second-conjugation verb, drop the -aigh of the root and add -óidh: brostaigh gives brostóidh sé, ceannaigh gives ceannóidh mé. The book shows this by placing each command beside the answer to Cad é a dhéanfaidh sé? (the book prints Céard a dhéanfaidh sé?).

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an dara réimniú, briathra caola (-igh)
rulesUlster.statement: For a slender second-conjugation verb, drop the -igh and add -eoidh: bailigh gives baileoidh sé, mínigh gives míneoidh sé, dúisigh gives dúiseoidh sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, ceist agus diúltach
rulesUlster.statement: The question is formed with An and eclipsis (An gceannóidh tú? An mbaileoidh sé?) and the negative with Ní and lenition (Ní cheannóidh mé, Ní bhaileoidh mé). The answer repeats the verb: Ceannóidh mé / Ní cheannóidh mé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an chéad phearsa iolra
rulesUlster.statement: The book gives the synthetic first person plural, -óimid / -eoimid (Ceannóimid, Baileoimid), as the answer to a question with sibh. In Ulster usage the first person plural is analytic, verb plus muid: ceannóidh muid, baileoidh muid, ní cheannóidh muid, ní bhaileoidh muid. The question with sibh is answered Ceannóidh muid / Ní cheannóidh muid.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form ends in -ófar for broad verbs and -eofar for slender verbs: ceannófar, baileofar. It takes eclipsis after An (An gceannófar?) and lenition after Ní (Ní cheannófar). In an exercise sentence the bracketed root is replaced by this form: (Ceannaigh) an carr gives Ceannófar an carr.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A second-conjugation verb beginning with a vowel behaves the same in the future (aeraigh gives aeróidh, éirigh gives éireoidh) but takes no d' and shows no change after An or Ní: An ullmhóidh tú? Ní ullmhóidh mé, An aimseoidh sé? Ní aimseoidh sé, An ullmhófar? Ní ullmhófar.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, briathra a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A second-conjugation verb beginning with f takes the eclipsis bhf after An (An bhfiosróidh tú? An bhfiosrófar?) and the lenition fh after Ní (Ní fhiosróidh mé, Ní fhiosrófar). The book prints Ar bhfiosróidh tú? on page 45; this is a misprint for An bhfiosróidh tú?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, clásal le má agus nuair a
rulesUlster.statement: In the exercise sentences the main verb goes into the future while the verb after má stays in the present (Beannóidh mé do chara má fheicim é, Maróidh an cat an luch má fheiceann sé í); after nuair a the book uses the present (nuair a chloiseann sé mé; in Ulster nuair a chluineann sé mé) and also the future (nuair a bheidh am acu). Where the má clause has a synthetic first person plural (má chuirimid, má dhéanaimid, má théimid) Ulster usage is analytic: má chuireann muid, má dhéanann muid, má théann muid. The pupil changes only the bracketed verb.

rulesUlster.point: an dara réimniú, achoimre ar na haimsirí (láithreach, caite, fháistineach)
rulesUlster.statement: The summary table sets the three tenses side by side for five model verbs (ceannaigh, bailigh, ullmhaigh, aimsigh, fiosraigh). Present: -aím / -ím with the -aíonn / -íonn endings and the autonomous -aítear / -ítear, the first person plural in Ulster being ceannaíonn muid rather than ceannaímid; past: the root lenited, d' before a vowel or f (D'ullmhaigh, D'fhiosraigh), the autonomous -aíodh / -íodh, Níor / Ar, and in Ulster cheannaigh muid rather than cheannaíomar; future: -óidh / -eoidh, the autonomous -ófar / -eofar, Ní / An, and in Ulster ceannóidh muid rather than ceannóimid. The first person singular stays synthetic in every tense: ceannaím, cheannaigh mé, ceannóidh mé.

rulesUlster.point: an dara réimniú, an chéad phearsa iolra san aimsir chaite
rulesUlster.statement: The table gives the past first person plural synthetically: Cheannaíomar, Bhailíomar, D'ullmhaíomar, D'aimsíomar, D'fhiosraíomar. In Ulster usage these are analytic: cheannaigh muid, bhailigh muid, d'ullmhaigh muid, d'aimsigh muid, d'fhiosraigh muid; negative níor cheannaigh muid, question ar cheannaigh sibh?

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, briathra leathana an dara réimniú
rulesUlster.statement: The verbal noun of a broad -aigh verb is usually formed by replacing -aigh with -ú (aeraigh: aerú, ceartaigh: ceartú, socraigh: socrú). The list marks the exceptions ending in -ach (ceannach, clúdach, cnuasach, cuardach, cumhdach, fuadach), in -aí (corraí, fiafraí, ionsaí) and admháil.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, briathra leathana an dara réimniú
rulesUlster.statement: The verbal adjective of a broad -aigh verb replaces -aigh with -aithe (ceannaithe, críochnaithe, socraithe). The one exception in the list is dathaigh: daite.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha agus an aidiacht bhriathartha, briathra caola an dara réimniú
rulesUlster.statement: The verbal noun of a slender -igh verb is usually -iú (aimsiú, ceistiú, deisiú, míniú) and the verbal adjective -ithe (aimsithe, deisithe, mínithe). The list marks the exceptions: biseach, coinneáil, cuimhneamh, dúiseacht, éirí, glinniúint, imeacht, impí, réiteach, taifeach.

rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir chaite: na foirmeacha dearfacha
rulesUlster.statement: The eleven irregular verbs have their own past-tense stems which must be learned: beir gives rug, clois gives chuala, tar gives tháinig, ith gives d'ith, tabhair gives thug, déan gives rinne, feic gives chonaic, abair gives dúirt, téigh gives chuaigh, faigh gives fuair, bí gives bhí. The book presents them through a short story and a table of question and answer pairs. In the app the first person plural is rug muid, chuala muid, tháinig muid, d'ith muid, thug muid, rinne muid, chonaic muid, dúirt muid, chuaigh muid, fuair muid, bhí muid.

rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir chaite: an fhoirm dhiúltach agus an fhoirm cheisteach
rulesUlster.statement: Five verbs behave like regular verbs and take níor and ar with the same stem as the positive form: níor rug, ar rug; níor chuala, ar chuala; níor tháinig, ar tháinig; níor ith, ar ith; níor thug, ar thug. The other six take ní and an with a separate dependent form: ní dhearna, an ndearna; ní fhaca, an bhfaca; ní dúirt, an ndúirt; ní dheachaigh, an ndeachaigh; ní bhfuair, an bhfuair; ní raibh, an raibh. With muid the same pattern holds: níor rug muid, ar rug muid; ní dhearna muid, an ndearna muid.

rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir chaite: freagra ar cheist
rulesUlster.statement: A yes or no question in the past tense is answered by repeating the verb in the positive or negative form, without a word for yes or no: Ar tháinig tú ar scoil ar do rothar? Tháinig mé. Níor tháinig mé. An bhfaca tú an scannán sin? Chonaic mé. Ní fhaca mé.

rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir chaite: an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: Each irregular verb has a past-tense autonomous form: rugadh, chualathas, thángthas, itheadh, tugadh, rinneadh, chonacthas, dúradh, chuathas, fuarthas, bhíothas. The negative and question forms use the same particle as the verb itself takes: níor rugadh, ar rugadh; ní dhearnadh, an ndearnadh; ní fhacthas, an bhfacthas; ní dúradh, an ndúradh; ní dheachthas, an ndeachthas; ní bhfuarthas, an bhfuarthas; ní rabhthas, an rabhthas.

rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir chaite: an chéad phearsa iolra (nóta Uladh, ní ón leabhar)
rulesUlster.statement: House adaptation, applied throughout this section: the book's synthetic first person plural (rugamar, chualamar, thángamar, d'itheamar, thugamar, rinneamar, chonaiceamar, dúramar, chuamar, fuaireamar, bhíomar) is given as rug muid, chuala muid, tháinig muid, d'ith muid, thug muid, rinne muid, chonaic muid, dúirt muid, chuaigh muid, fuair muid, bhí muid, with negatives níor rug muid, níor tháinig muid, níor ith muid, ní dhearna muid, ní fhaca muid, ní dheachaigh muid. Exercise B and C items containing the synthetic forms have been adjusted the same way. The book's eclipsis after preposition and article (ar an ngadaí, ar an mbus) is given as ar an ghadaí, ar an bhus. Vocabulary changed: ag féachaint ar becomes ag amharc ar, le déanaí becomes ar na mallaibh, fós becomes go fóill. The standard autonomous forms chualathas, thángthas, chonacthas, chuathas and bhíothas are kept because they are the written exam forms, although they are rare in Ulster speech; flagged for the principal in case he prefers to teach only the commoner ones (rugadh, tugadh, rinneadh, dúradh, fuarthas).

rulesUlster.point: an saorbhriathar: sampla lochtach sa leabhar
rulesUlster.statement: Flag: the worked example for exercise D on page 50 is printed as two bracketed stems, (Deir) leo a bheith ciúin and (Abair) leo a bheith ciúin, with no completed answer shown. rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir láithreach: na haon bhriathar déag
rulesUlster.statement: The book treats eleven irregular verbs in the present tense: beir, clois, tar, ith, tabhair, déan, feic, abair, téigh, faigh and bí. Each has a present stem that may differ from the root (tar gives tagann, tabhair gives tugann, abair gives deir, téigh gives téann, and in Ulster feic gives tchí: tchím, tchí tú, tchí sé, tchí muid). The first person singular keeps the synthetic ending -im (beirim, cloisim, tagaim), the other persons take -eann/-ann with a pronoun, and the first person plural is analytic: beireann muid, cloiseann muid, tagann muid, tá muid, not beirimid, cloisimid, tagaimid, táimid.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an fhoirm cheisteach: An + urú
rulesUlster.statement: A present-tense question is formed with An followed by eclipsis of the verb: An mbeireann, An gcloiseann, An dtagann, An dtugann, An ndéanann, An bhfeiceann, An ndeir, An dtéann, An bhfaigheann. A verb beginning with a vowel takes no change (An itheann), and bí has its own dependent form (An bhfuil). Note that feic uses the dependent form after An even in Ulster: the answer is Tchím or Tchí sé, but the question is An bhfeiceann tú? and An bhfeiceann sé?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an fhoirm dhiúltach: Ní + séimhiú
rulesUlster.statement: The negative is formed with Ní followed by lenition of the verb: Ní bheireann, Ní chloiseann, Ní thagann, Ní thugann, Ní dhéanann, Ní fheiceann, Ní théann, Ní fhaigheann. Deir is not lenited (Ní deir), a vowel takes no change (Ní itheann), and bí has the separate negative form Níl. Feic again uses the dependent form after Ní: Tchí sé but Ní fheiceann sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, freagra gairid
rulesUlster.statement: A yes/no question is answered by repeating the verb with the pronoun, without any word for yes or no: An gcloiseann sé? gives Cloiseann sé or Ní chloiseann sé; An bhfuil sé go maith? gives Tá sé or Níl sé. With feic the positive answer is the independent Ulster form and the negative the dependent one: An bhfeiceann tú? gives Tchím or Ní fheicim; An bhfeiceann sé? gives Tchí sé or Ní fheiceann sé. In the first person plural the answer is Cloiseann muid, Tá muid, Níl muid.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form (saorbhriathar) of the present tense is made with -tear or -tar on the stem (beirtear, cloistear, tagtar, tugtar, déantar, feictear, deirtear, téitear, faightear), with itear for ith and táthar for bí. Its negative and question forms follow the same rules as the rest of the verb: Ní bheirtear, An mbeirtear? and, for bí, Níltear. Feictear is the form to teach; the Ulster tchítear is also heard.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir láithreach, bí: tá, níl, an bhfuil
rulesUlster.statement: Bí is the only verb with three distinct present forms: tá in the positive, níl in the negative and bhfuil after the question particle An. The forms to teach are Tá mé, Tá tú, Tá sé/sí, Tá muid, Tá sibh, Tá siad and Níl mé, Níl muid; the book's Táim, Nílim, Táimid and Nílimid are standard forms pupils will meet in print but should not be asked to produce.

paradigmsUlster.title: Feic, an aimsir láithreach (dearfach, diúltach, ceisteach). The book gives the standard Feicim, Feiceann tú, Feiceann sé/sí, Feicimid, Feiceann sibh, Feiceann siad. The independent forms are replaced here by the Ulster tchí (tchím, tchí tú, tchí sé/sí, tchí muid, tchí sibh, tchí siad); the dependent forms after Ní and An stay as in the book (Ní fheicim, An bhfeicim?). Principal to confirm tchí sé rather than the newer tchíonn sé, and whether to show tchítear beside feictear
forms: Tchím | Tchí muid | Ní fheicim | An bhfeicim?
SB Feictear (Ulaidh fosta: tchítear) | Ní fheictear | An bhfeictear?

paradigmsUlster.title: Abair, an aimsir láithreach (dearfach, diúltach, ceisteach)
forms: Deirim | Deir muid | Ní deirim | An ndeirim?
SB Deirtear | Ní deirtear | An ndeirtear?

paradigmsUlster.title: Téigh, an aimsir láithreach (dearfach, diúltach, ceisteach)
forms: Téim | Téann muid | Ní théim | An dtéim?
SB Téitear | Ní théitear | An dtéitear?

paradigmsUlster.title: Faigh, an aimsir láithreach (dearfach, diúltach, ceisteach)
forms: Faighim | Faigheann muid | Ní fhaighim | An bhfaighim?
SB Faightear | Ní fhaightear | An bhfaightear?

paradigmsUlster.title: Bí, an aimsir láithreach (dearfach, diúltach, ceisteach)
forms: Tá mé | Tá muid | Níl mé | Níl muid | An bhfuil mé?
Tá tú | Tá sibh | Níl tú | Níl sibh
Tá sé/sí | Tá siad | Níl sé/sí | Níl siad

sentences.original: Cloiseann Pól an clog ag bualadh.

sentences.ulster: Deir mamaí leis éirí.

sentences.original: Tagann sé anuas go dtí an chistin agus itheann sé a bhricfeasta.

sentences.original: Déanann mamaí an lón agus tugann sí dó é.

sentences.original: Beireann sé ar a lón agus faigheann sé a mhála.

sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, beir agus faigh

sentences.original: Téann sé amach as an teach agus feiceann sé a chara Seán.

sentences.ulster: Tá rothar ag Seán.
sentences.fresh: Tá fón póca ag Niamh.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, bí
sentences.note: No Ulster change.

sentences.original: 1. An gcloiseann sé an clog ag bualadh gach maidin?
sentences.ulster: An gcloiseann sé an clog ag bualadh achan mhaidin? Cloiseann sé. / Ní chloiseann sé.
sentences.fresh: An gcloiseann sé an fón ag bualadh achan mhaidin? Cloiseann sé. / Ní chloiseann sé.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, clois: ceist agus freagra gairid, dearfach agus diúltach
sentences.note: gach maidin becomes achan mhaidin (achan lenites). Short answers shown after the question as in the book.

sentences.original: 2. An ndeir sí sin leat go minic?
sentences.ulster: An ndeir sí sin leat go minic? Deir sí. / Ní deir sí.
sentences.fresh: An ndeir sí sin leat ar an fhón go minic? Deir sí. / Ní deir sí.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, abair (deir): ceist agus freagra gairid; ní shéimhítear deir
sentences.note: No Ulster change to the verb; fresh sentence adds ar an fhón (lenition after preposition and article).

sentences.original: 3. An dtagann sé ar an mbus?
sentences.ulster: An dtagann sé ar an bhus? Tagann sé. / Ní thagann sé.
sentences.fresh: An dtagann sé ar scoil ar an bhus? Tagann sé. / Ní thagann sé.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, tar (tagann): ceist agus freagra gairid (Ulaidh: ar an bhus)
sentences.note: ar an mbus becomes ar an bhus.

sentences.ulster: An ndéanann sí a dícheall? Déanann sí. / Ní dhéanann sí.
sentences.fresh: An ndéanann sí a dícheall sa rang Gaeilge? Déanann sí. / Ní dhéanann sí.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, déan: ceist agus freagra gairid
sentences.note: No Ulster change.

sentences.ulster: An dtugann sé cabhair di? Tugann sé. / Ní thugann sé.
sentences.fresh: An dtugann sé cabhair di leis an obair bhaile? Tugann sé. / Ní thugann sé.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, tabhair (tugann): ceist agus freagra gairid
sentences.note: The book's dí is the older spelling; di is used. Cuidiú would be the more Ulster word for cabhair but cabhair is kept as conservative usage.

sentences.ulster: An itheann sé cáis? Itheann sé. / Ní itheann sé.
sentences.fresh: An itheann sé úll ag am sosa? Itheann sé. / Ní itheann sé.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, ith: ceist agus freagra gairid; guta, gan urú gan séimhiú (the book misprints the positive answer as 'Iteann sé')
sentences.note: Misprint Iteann corrected to Itheann.

sentences.ulster: An mbeireann cat ar lucha? Beireann sé. / Ní bheireann sé.
sentences.fresh: An mbeireann an madadh ar an liathróid? Beireann sé. / Ní bheireann sé.
sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, beir: ceist agus freagra gairid
sentences.note: Ulster would more often say luchóga for lucha; kept as in the book, principal to decide.

sentences.original: 8. An bhfaigheann sé litir go minic?

sentences.ulster: An bhfuil sé go maith? Tá sé. / Níl sé.

sentences.point: an aimsir láithreach, bí: an bhfuil, tá, níl
sentences.note: Fresh sentence adds ag an pheil (lenition after preposition and article).

sentences.original: 11. An bhfeiceann sé a aintín go minic?

sentences.note: Positive answer Tchí sé (checker's correction applied for consistency with the paradigm; earlier Tchíonn sé), negative keeps the dependent form Ní fheiceann sé; principal to confirm.

rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir fháistineach: na fréamhacha
rulesUlster.statement: The eleven irregular verbs take a changed stem in the future: beir gives béarfaidh, clois gives cloisfidh, tar gives tiocfaidh, ith gives íosfaidh, tabhair gives tabharfaidh, déan gives déanfaidh, feic gives feicfidh, abair gives déarfaidh, téigh gives rachaidh, faigh gives gheobhaidh, bí gives beidh. The book teaches them through a short story about Pól's morning and then through question and answer pairs. The stems are the same in Ulster; only the first person plural ending differs (see below). Donegal speakers also say tchífidh mé for feicfidh mé, but the app keeps feicfidh as the form pupils write.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an fhoirm dhiúltach
rulesUlster.statement: The negative is formed with ní, which lenites the verb (ní chloisfidh, ní thiocfaidh, ní thabharfaidh, ní dhéanfaidh, ní fheicfidh, ní bhéarfaidh, ní bheidh). Ní does not change déarfaidh or rachaidh, and it cannot lenite a vowel (ní íosfaidh); faigh alone uses its dependent form with eclipsis after ní: ní bhfaighidh. The local negative cha is not used in the app; pupils write ní.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an fhoirm cheisteach
rulesUlster.statement: The question is formed with an, which eclipses the verb (an gcloisfidh, an dtiocfaidh, an mbéarfaidh, an ndéanfaidh, an dtabharfaidh, an bhfeicfidh, an ndéarfaidh, an mbeidh). Rachaidh and íosfaidh are unchanged after an, and faigh again takes its dependent form: an bhfaighidh.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir fháistineach, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form ends in -far or -fear according to the stem: béarfar, cloisfear, tiocfar, íosfar, tabharfar, déanfar, feicfear, déarfar, rachfar, beifear. Faigh has gheofar in the positive but ní bhfaighfear and an bhfaighfear in the negative and question. Negative and question forms follow the same lenition and eclipsis pattern as the personal forms.

rulesUlster.point: freagra ar cheist san aimsir fháistineach
rulesUlster.statement: A yes or no question is answered by repeating the verb in its positive or negative form with the right pronoun (An dtiocfaidh tú liom? Tiocfaidh mé. Ní thiocfaidh mé.); there is no separate word for yes or no. A question to sibh is answered with muid: An rachaidh sibh? Rachaidh muid. Ní rachaidh muid.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad phearsa iolra: foirmeacha Uladh
rulesUlster.statement: The book prints the synthetic first person plural (béarfaimid, rachaimid, beimid). In Ulster the analytic form is used: béarfaidh muid, cloisfidh muid, tiocfaidh muid, íosfaidh muid, tabharfaidh muid, déanfaidh muid, feicfidh muid, déarfaidh muid, rachaidh muid, gheobhaidh muid, beidh muid; negative ní bhéarfaidh muid, ní bhfaighidh muid, ní bheidh muid; question an mbéarfaidh muid?, an mbeidh muid? The app uses muid in every answer and in every fresh stem (tar:muid, bí:muid), while the book's own wording (sinn, rachaimid) is kept only in the original stems and prompts.

rulesUlster.point: botúin chló sa tábla ar leathanach 58 (le seiceáil)
rulesUlster.statement: Flag for the principal: the printed table contains errors that are the book's, not the scanner's, and they were confirmed against the page image. Under Tar the question column reads An gcloisfear? where An dtiocfaidh mé? is meant; under Feic the first form is printed Feicidh mé for Feicfidh mé and the question column reads An bhfeicfear? where An bhfeicfidh mé? is meant; under Téigh the question column reads An rachfar? where An rachaidh mé? is meant; under Faigh the tú and sibh forms are printed Geobhaidh without lenition; the question An íosfar lacks its question mark. Three smaller misprints are silently normalised: the heading Teigh is printed without a fada, the Tabhair rows for sé/sí, sibh and siad are printed with a lowercase initial, and exercise D 2 on page 57 is printed Deánfaimid with the fada on the wrong vowel. Also on page 55 question 6 is printed in the conditional (An íosfadh tú ... Ní íosfadh mé) where the future íosfaidh is meant. The Ulster paradigms below give the corrected forms; the book's misprints are recorded only in the original paradigms.

rulesUlster.point: urú i ndiaidh réamhfhocail agus an ailt sna ceachtanna (le seiceáil)
rulesUlster.statement: Flag for the principal: two exercise stems carry the standard eclipsis after preposition and article, ar an mbata (page 56, A 7) and ag an gcruinniú (page 57, E 1). In the Ulster versions these become ar an bhata and ag an chruinniú, following the school rule that a simple preposition and the singular article lenite (ar an bhord, ag an doras, sa charr, leis an mhúinteoir). The fresh sentences use the Ulster pattern throughout (ag an chluiche, ar an bhus, ar an ghadaí). The original stems keep the book's wording.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht shealbhach, mo, do, a (sé): séimhiú
rulesUlster.statement: The possessive adjectives mo (my), do (your, singular) and a (his) lenite the first consonant of the following noun: mo theach, do chóta, a bhróga.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht shealbhach, mo agus do roimh ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: Before a vowel or fh, mo and do drop their vowel and become m' and d': m'fhiacail, m'uncail, m'aintín, d'athair.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht shealbhach, a (sí): h roimh ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: The possessive a meaning her causes no change to a consonant (a cara, a bronntanas) but puts h before a vowel: a hordóg.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht shealbhach, a (sé) roimh ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: The possessive a meaning his causes no change before a vowel: a ordóg.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht shealbhach, ár, bhur, a (siad): urú
rulesUlster.statement: The plural possessives ár (our), bhur (your, plural) and a (their) eclipse the following consonant: ár gcóipleabhair, bhur dtuismitheoirí, a gcótaí. Before a vowel they add n- (written nA without a hyphen before a capital): ár nAthair, bhur n-aintín, a n-uncail.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht shealbhach le hainmneacha briathartha staide: i mo chónaí, ina suí
rulesUlster.statement: The states cónaí, dúiseacht, suí, seasamh, tost, luí and codladh are expressed with the preposition i plus the possessive adjective: i mo, i do, ina (his and her), inár, in bhur (also written i bhur), ina (their). The usual lenition, h and eclipsis rules of the possessives apply: i mo chónaí, ina chónaí, ina cónaí, inár gcónaí, ina gcodladh. In Ulster the first person plural verb is analytic: tá muid inár gcónaí, not táimid inár gcónaí.

rulesUlster.point: na maoluimhreacha: cruth agus úsáid
rulesUlster.statement: Counting numbers used on their own take the particle a before them (a haon, a dó) and a vowel-initial number takes h (a haon, a hocht); 11 to 19 add déag (a dó dhéag is lenited), 20 is fiche and 21 is fiche a haon. These forms are used for labels such as rang a trí, seomra a hocht, bus a hocht and, in a Northern Ireland school, Bliain a hocht for Year 8. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na deicheanna agus an céad
rulesUlster.statement: The tens are deich, fiche, tríocha, daichead, caoga, seasca, seachtó, ochtó, nócha and céad, and a noun following a ten is unchanged (fiche punt, seasca punt, seachtó pingin), while deich eclipses (deich bpunt, deich bpingin). Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: an mhatamaitic: suimiú, dealú, iolrú, roinnt
rulesUlster.statement: Sums are read with is for plus (a seacht is a dó), óna for minus (a trí óna hocht), faoina for times (a sé faoina trí), ar for divided by (fiche ar a dó) and sin for equals. The book prints the division example as 20 + 2 = 10, a misprint for 20 divided by 2 (confirmed in the page image). Ulster usage is the same as the standard; roinnte ar is also heard for divided by.

rulesUlster.point: an t-am: an uair a chlog
rulesUlster.statement: The hours are given as Tá sé a haon a chlog, Tá sé a dó a chlog and so on up to a dó dhéag a chlog; the counting form with a is used, with h before aon and ocht. The book prints a h-aon and a dó-dhéag with hyphens, an older spelling. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: an t-am: leathuair, ceathrú, bomaite
rulesUlster.statement: Minutes past the hour use tar éis (leathuair tar éis a deich, ceathrú tar éis a naoi) and minutes to the hour use chun (fiche bomaite chun a trí, cúig bhomaite chun a cúig); the word bomaite may be left out. Ulster uses bomaite where the standard has nóiméad: it is lenited after 2 to 6 (cúig bhomaite) and eclipsed after 7 to 10 (deich mbomaite). Many Ulster speakers say i ndiaidh for tar éis and go dtí for chun (leathuair i ndiaidh a deich, fiche bomaite go dtí a trí); the app keeps tar éis and chun as the standard forms and the principal may prefer the Ulster ones.

rulesUlster.point: na bunuimhreacha: séimhiú agus urú ar an ainmfhocal
rulesUlster.statement: A noun after a cardinal number stays singular. One is aon chapall amháin or capall amháin; 2 to 6 lenite (dhá chapall, sé chapall); 7 to 9 eclipse (seacht gcapall, naoi gcapall); deich also eclipses (deich gcapall) and is listed as an exception to the 7 to 9 rule. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na bunuimhreacha: 11 go 19, 20 agus os a chionn
rulesUlster.statement: For 11 to 19 the noun sits between the number and déag (aon chapall déag, seacht gcapall déag); 20 is fiche capall with no mutation; above 20 the unit and noun come first and the ten follows with is (aon chapall is fiche or capall is fiche, ocht gcapall is tríocha, trí chapall is caoga). Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na bunuimhreacha: ainmfhocail a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A vowel-initial noun is unchanged after 2 to 6 (dhá úll, trí iasc, sé uan) but takes n- after 7 to 9 (seacht n-úll, ocht n-iasc, naoi n-uan). Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na bunuimhreacha: dhá agus ceithre i gcomparáid
rulesUlster.statement: The picture captions contrast dhá bhuidéal with dhá iasc and ceithre chos with ceithre úll to show that 2 to 6 lenite a consonant but leave a vowel untouched. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: airgead: punt agus pingin
rulesUlster.statement: Prices are read with the noun singular after the number: punt (amháin), ceithre phunt, sé phunt nócha a naoi for £6.99, deich bpingin for 10p, cúig phunt déag for £15. The Ulster question is Cá mhéad atá air? (the book also gives Cé mhéad atá air?). The book treats pingin as an ordinary noun, and the app follows the book: it is lenited after 2 to 6 (trí phingin, sé phingin is fiche) and eclipsed after 7 to 10 (ocht bpingin, deich bpingin), and unchanged after the tens (seachtó pingin). The standard special plural pingine after 3 to 10 (trí pingine, sé pingine is fiche) is not used in the book; the principal should confirm which the app teaches, and the sentences will follow that choice.

rulesUlster.point: na horduimhreacha 1ú go 20ú
rulesUlster.statement: Ordinals are an chéad chapall (chéad lenites the noun), an dara, an tríú, an ceathrú, an cúigiú, an séú, an seachtú, an t-ochtú, an naoú, an deichiú; a vowel-initial ordinal takes t- after an (an t-aonú, an t-ochtú). From 11th to 19th the ordinal comes first and déag follows the noun (an t-aonú capall déag, an dóú capall déag); 20th is an fichiú capall. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na horduimhreacha os cionn 20
rulesUlster.statement: Above 20 the unit ordinal comes first, then the noun, then is and the ten (an t-aonú capall is fiche, an dara capall is fiche, an tríú capall is tríocha, an t-ochtú capall is daichead). The tens are an tríochadú, an daicheadú, an caogadú, an seascadú, an seachtódú, an t-ochtódú, an nóchadú and an céadú capall. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na huimhreacha pearsanta 1 go 14
rulesUlster.statement: People are counted with the personal numbers duine, beirt, triúr, ceathrar, cúigear, seisear, seachtar, ochtar, naonúr, deichniúr; from 11 the ordinary numbers are used with duine and dhéag: aon duine dhéag, dáréag (12), trí dhuine dhéag, ceithre dhuine dhéag. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na huimhreacha pearsanta le hainmfhocal
rulesUlster.statement: A noun after a personal number is in the genitive plural: beirt lenites (beirt fhear, beirt bhan) but triúr to deichniúr do not (triúr fear, ceathrar ban, deichniúr fear). From 11 the ordinary cardinals are used with the noun singular: aon fhear déag, dáréag fear, trí fhear déag, seacht bhfear déag, fiche fear. Ulster usage is the same as the standard; gasúr and girseach may be used beside buachaill and cailín (beirt ghasúr, triúr girseach).

rulesUlster.point: na huimhreacha pearsanta os cionn 20
rulesUlster.statement: Above 20 people are counted with the ordinary cardinals and duine: duine is fiche, trí dhuine is tríocha, ceithre dhuine is daichead, seacht nduine is caoga, naoi nduine is seasca, ocht nduine is ochtó, céad duine. Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na dátaí
rulesUlster.statement: A date is the ordinal, lá, then de and the month lenited: an tríú lá de Mhárta, an cúigiú lá déag de Bhealtaine; the same pattern serves for other months (d'Eanáir, d'Fheabhra, de Nollaig). Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: na horduimhreacha: cibé athrú is gá
rulesUlster.statement: When an ordinal is written out after an, the necessary changes are: t- before a vowel-initial ordinal (an t-aonú, an t-ochtú), lenition of the noun after an chéad (an chéad duais) and h before a vowel-initial noun after other ordinals (an fichiú huair, an t-aonú himleabhar déag). Ulster usage is the same as the standard.

rulesUlster.point: an dobhriathar: treo agus suíomh
rulesUlster.statement: Irish uses different adverbs for the direction of a movement and for the position where something rests afterwards. The section (subtitled Treo agus suíomh) teaches four groups of these adverbs through pairs of pictures: one showing the movement, the next showing the resting position. Ulster Irish uses exactly the same ten adverbs with the same meanings.

rulesUlster.point: suas, thuas, anuas
rulesUlster.statement: Suas is used for movement upwards away from the speaker (Tá Pól ag dul suas an staighre); thuas for being at rest up above (tá sé thuas staighre); anuas for movement downwards towards the speaker from above (Tá sé ag teacht anuas).

rulesUlster.point: síos, thíos, aníos
rulesUlster.statement: Síos is used for movement downwards away from the speaker (ag dul síos go bun an chnoic); thíos for being at rest down below (tá sí thíos ag bun an chnoic); aníos for movement upwards towards the speaker from below (ag teacht aníos arís).

rulesUlster.point: isteach, istigh
rulesUlster.statement: Isteach is used for movement into a place (Chuaigh Aoife isteach sa teach); istigh for being at rest inside (Anois tá sí istigh).

rulesUlster.point: amach, amuigh
rulesUlster.statement: Amach is used for movement out of a place (Shiúil Máirtín amach as an teach); amuigh for being at rest outside (tá sé amuigh sa ghairdín).

rulesUlster.point: nóta eagarthóireachta (not a rule of the book)
rulesUlster.statement: Flags for sign-off: the book's older spellings gháirdín and ina h-aonar have been modernised to ghairdín and ina haonar in the Ulster versions (gairdín is the app's own spelling); exercise item 10 now reads madadh for the book's madra; item 5 keeps déanach although mall is the more usual Ulster word for late, so the principal may prefer mall; items 7, 8 and 9 accept more than one adverb (thíos or thuas; suas or síos) and the answers given follow the most natural reading of the preceding item. No verb ending or article lenition in this section needed changing: sa teach, sa chistin, sa rang, as an teach are the same in Ulster and in the standard. Newry is written An tIúr (go dtí an tIúr) in the fresh sentences.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, an chéad réimniú, briathra leathana
rulesUlster.statement: To form the conditional of a broad first-conjugation verb, lenite the initial consonant and add -fadh to the root for the third person (dún becomes dhúnfadh sé). Illustrated by the book's paired lists of commands and conditional sentences, headed Cad é a dhéanfadh sé? in Ulster usage.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, foircinn na mbriathra leathana
rulesUlster.statement: The broad endings are -fainn (mé), -fá (tú), -fadh sé / sí, -fadh muid (the book's -faimis), -fadh sibh, -faidís (siad) and -faí (saorbhriathar). Questions to sibh are answered with the muid form (An ndúnfadh sibh? Dhúnfadh muid). Only the first person singular keeps a synthetic ending in Ulster school usage.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, an chéad réimniú, briathra caola
rulesUlster.statement: A slender-root verb takes the same endings spelt slender: -feadh (chuirfeadh sé), -finn, -feá, -feadh muid (the book's -fimis), -fidís, -fí.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, ceist agus diúltach
rulesUlster.statement: A question is formed with An plus eclipsis (An ndúnfá? An gcuirfeá?) and the negative with Ní plus lenition (Ní dhúnfainn, Ní chuirfinn). Yes and no answers repeat the verb in the right person.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with a vowel takes d' in the positive (D'ólfadh sé, D'úsáidfeadh sé) but drops it after An and Ní (An ólfá? D'ólfainn / Ní ólfainn).

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, briathra a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with f takes d' plus lenition in the positive (D'fhágfadh sé), eclipsis after An (An bhfágfá?) and lenition without d' after Ní (Ní fhágfainn).

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form ends in -faí (broad) or -fí (slender), is lenited in the positive, and takes d' before a vowel or f (Dhúnfaí, Chuirfí, D'ólfaí, D'fhágfaí; Ní dhúnfaí, Ní ólfaí). Exercise E applies it: (mol) na páistí becomes Mholfaí na páistí.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, clásal le dá
rulesUlster.statement: A condition introduced by dá takes the conditional in both halves: Dá mbeadh tart orm d'ólfainn tae; Dá mbeinn tinn d'fhanfainn sa leaba; dá mbeifeá tinn; dá mbeidís go maith. These forms of bí are the same in Ulster school usage.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, an fhoirm dhiúltach
rulesUlster.statement: To make a conditional form negative, put Ní before it, remove any d' and lenite the initial consonant: Mholfadh muid becomes Ní mholfadh muid, D'éistfidís becomes Ní éistfidís, D'fhéachfadh sé becomes Ní fhéachfadh sé (in Ulster the verb amharc is more usual than féach: D'amharcfadh sé, Ní amharcfadh sé).

rulesUlster.point: nóta Uladh: an chéad phearsa iolra
rulesUlster.statement: Applied throughout the Ulster fields: the book's synthetic first person plural (dhúnfaimis, chuirfimis, d'fhéachfaimis, mholfaimis, chaillfimis) is dhúnfadh muid, chuirfeadh muid, d'fhéachfadh muid, mholfadh muid, chaillfeadh muid. The first person singular -fainn / -finn stays synthetic. Still for sign-off.

rulesUlster.point: nóta Uladh: urú i ndiaidh an ailt
rulesUlster.statement: Applied throughout the Ulster fields: ar an bhord, ar an chlár dubh, ar an phictiúr, sa charr, leis an cheol, as an bhus; d, t and s stay unchanged (ar an doras, ar an teilifís, sa teach). Céard a dhéanfadh sé? and Cad a dhéanfá? become Cad é a dhéanfadh sé? and Cad é a dhéanfá?. Féach ar becomes Amharc ar except where the book is deliberately illustrating an f-initial verb; those items are flagged.

rulesUlster.point: nóta eagarthóireachta: earráidí cló sa leabhar
rulesUlster.statement: Checked against the page images: the book prints Mhúchfadh sé an soilse (p76), (glan) na seomra, ar an teilfís, (gearr) an ciste and Da mbeadh foclóir (p79). The data reads na soilse, na seomraí, ar an teilifís, an císte and Dá mbeadh. The worked example for exercise A (Freagair na ceisteanna, item 1, p78) also has a stray capital in ní Dhéanfainn. rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an chéad réimniú, briathra leathana
rulesUlster.statement: To form the habitual past of a broad first-conjugation verb, lenite the initial consonant and add the endings: -ainn (mé), -tá (tú), -adh sé/sí, -adh muid, -adh sibh, -aidís (siad). The order form Dún gives Dhúnainn, Dhúntá, Dhúnadh sé, Dhúnadh muid, Dhúnadh sibh, Dhúnaidís. (The standard has the synthetic Dhúnaimis for the first person plural.)

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an chéad réimniú, briathra caola
rulesUlster.statement: A slender first-conjugation verb takes the same pattern with slender spellings of the endings: -inn, -teá, -eadh sé/sí, -eadh muid, -eadh sibh, -idís. Cuir gives Chuirinn, Chuirteá, Chuireadh sé, Chuireadh muid, Chuireadh sibh, Chuiridís. (The standard has Chuirimis.)

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an dara pearsa uatha
rulesUlster.statement: The second person singular has its own synthetic ending, -tá after a broad stem and -teá after a slender stem: Dhúntá, Chuirteá, D'óltá, D'úsáidteá, D'fhágtá. The pupil is expected to use it rather than dhúnadh tú.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an dara pearsa iolra
rulesUlster.statement: With sibh there is no synthetic ending: the third-person form is used with the pronoun, Dhúnadh sibh, Chuireadh sibh, D'óladh sibh. When the question is put with sibh, the answer is given in the first person plural with muid (An ndúnadh sibh? Dhúnadh muid). The standard answers Dhúnaimis.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A first-conjugation verb beginning with a vowel takes d' before it in the habitual past: Ól gives D'óladh sé, D'ólainn, D'óltá; Úsáid gives D'úsáideadh sé, D'úsáidinn. After Ní and An the d' is dropped and nothing is prefixed: Ní ólainn, An óltá?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, briathra a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A first-conjugation verb beginning with f is lenited and takes d' as well: Fág gives D'fhágadh sé, D'fhágainn, D'fhágtá. In the negative the d' is dropped but the lenition stays: Ní fhágadh sé, Ní fhágtaí. In the question the f is eclipsed: An bhfágtá? An bhfágaidís?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an fhoirm dhiúltach
rulesUlster.statement: The negative is formed with Ní, which lenites the verb: Ní dhúnainn, Ní chuireadh sé. With vowel and f verbs the d' disappears: Ní óladh muid, Ní úsáidtí, Ní fhágaidís. (The standard has Ní ólaimis for the first person plural.)

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an fhoirm cheisteach
rulesUlster.statement: The question is formed with An, which eclipses the verb: An ndúntá? An gcuireadh sé? An bhfágadh sibh? A vowel-initial verb takes no change after An: An óladh sí? An úsáidtí?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form (saorbhriathar) is made by leniting the verb and adding -taí to a broad stem or -tí to a slender stem: Dhúntaí, Chuirtí, D'óltaí, D'úsáidtí, D'fhágtaí, Bhaintí na barraí san fhómhar. Negative: Ní dhúntaí, Ní fhágtaí. Question: An ndúntaí? An bhfágtaí?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite agus an modh coinníollach, comparáid
rulesUlster.statement: The summary table sets the habitual past beside the conditional to show that they share the same set of person endings; the conditional simply has f (or fe) before them: Dhúnainn and Dhúnfainn, Dhúntá and Dhúnfá, Dhúnadh sé and Dhúnfadh sé, Dhúnadh muid and Dhúnfadh muid, Dhúntaí and Dhúnfaí. (The standard sets Dhúnaimis beside Dhúnfaimis.)

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an chéad phearsa iolra (nóta Ultach)
rulesUlster.statement: The book gives the synthetic first person plural, Dhúnaimis, Chuirimis, D'ólaimis. In Ulster school usage the analytic form with muid is used instead: dhúnadh muid, chuireadh muid, d'óladh muid, d'fhágadh muid, and in the negative ní dhúnadh muid, ní óladh muid. The first person singular stays synthetic: dhúnainn, chuirinn. The tables and answers in this section have been changed accordingly.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, an dara réimniú, briathra leathana (-aigh)
rulesUlster.statement: For a second-conjugation verb ending in a broad -aigh (brostaigh, ceannaigh, críochnaigh), drop the -aigh and add -ódh for the third person (Bhrostódh sé, Cheannódh sé), and lenite the initial consonant. The book teaches it from the order form: the pupil takes the ordú and turns it into what he would do (Cad é a dhéanfadh sé?).

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, an dara réimniú, briathra caola (-igh)
rulesUlster.statement: For a second-conjugation verb ending in a slender -igh (bailigh, mínigh, deisigh, dúisigh), drop the -igh and add -eodh (Bhaileodh sé, Mhíneodh sé), again with lenition of the initial consonant.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, na foirmeacha pearsanta (-óinn, -ófá, -óimis, -óidís, -ófaí)
rulesUlster.statement: The personal endings in Ulster school usage are -óinn (mé), -ófá (tú), -ódh sé/sí, -ódh muid, -ódh sibh, -ódh siad and -ófaí (saorbhriathar); slender verbs take -eoinn, -eofá, -eodh, -eodh muid, -eodh sibh, -eodh siad, -eofaí. The first person singular stays synthetic (Cheannóinn, Bhaileoinn). Where the book answers the sibh question with Cheannóimis or Bhaileoimis, the school form is Cheannódh muid, Bhaileodh muid. Where the book has -óidís (Cheannóidís), the school form used here is Cheannódh siad; the -óidís ending is also heard in Donegal and pupils should recognise it. Principal to confirm this choice.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, ceist agus diúltach (An + urú, Ní + séimhiú)
rulesUlster.statement: A question takes An and eclipses the verb (An gceannófá? An mbaileodh sé?); the negative takes Ní and lenites (Ní cheannóinn, Ní bhaileodh sé). The positive answer is the lenited form on its own (Cheannóinn, Bhaileodh sé). No change for Ulster; the app does not use the local cha.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A second-conjugation verb beginning with a vowel takes d' in the positive (D'aeródh sé, D'ullmhódh sé, D'aimseodh sé). After An there is no change and no d' (An ullmhófá? An aimseodh sé?), and after Ní there is no d' either (Ní ullmhóinn, Ní aimseodh sé).

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, briathra a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A second-conjugation verb beginning with f takes d'fh in the positive (D'fhiosródh sé, D'fholmhódh sé), bhf after An (An bhfiosrófá?) and fh after Ní (Ní fhiosróinn).

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, an saorbhriathar (-ófaí, -eofaí)
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form ends in -ófaí for broad verbs and -eofaí for slender verbs, with the same initial changes as the other persons: Cheannófaí, Bhaileofaí, D'ullmhófaí, D'aimseofaí, D'fhiosrófaí; An gceannófaí? Ní cheannófaí. Note: the sample answer printed for exercise C on page 88 is D'aontófar, which mixes the future ending with the conditional d'; in this section the intended form is D'aontófaí, and the answers below use -ófaí. Flag for the principal.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach, clásail choinníollacha (dá, mura)
rulesUlster.statement: The exercise sentences pair the conditional main verb with a dá clause or a mura clause. In Ulster school usage the plural forms inside those clauses are analytic too: dá mbeadh siad (book: dá mbeidís), dá gcuirfeadh siad (dá gcuirfidís), mura dtuigfeadh siad (mura dtuigfidís); dá mbeadh, dá mb'fhéidir leo, dá bhfeicfeadh sé, dá gcuirfinn and dá mbéarfadh sé are unchanged. The book does not state this as a rule, but every item in exercise A is built on it.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an dara réimniú: briathra in -aigh
rulesUlster.statement: To form the habitual past of a second-conjugation verb ending in -aigh, lenite the initial consonant and replace -aigh with -aíodh for sé/sí (Brostaigh becomes Bhrostaíodh sé, Ceannaigh becomes Cheannaíodh sé). The tense answers the question Cad é a dhéanadh sé? (what used he to do?).

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an dara réimniú: briathra in -igh
rulesUlster.statement: For a second-conjugation verb ending in -igh (slender), lenite and replace -igh with -íodh: Bailigh becomes Bhailíodh sé, Mínigh becomes Mhíníodh sé, Dúisigh becomes Dhúisíodh sé.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, na foircinn phearsanta
rulesUlster.statement: The endings are -aínn/-ínn (mé), -aíteá/-íteá (tú), -aíodh/-íodh sé or sí, -aíodh/-íodh muid, -aíodh/-íodh sibh, -aídís/-ídís (siad), with the saorbhriathar in -aítí/-ítí: Cheannaínn, Cheannaíteá, Cheannaíodh sé, Cheannaíodh muid, Cheannaíodh sibh, Cheannaídís, Cheannaítí. The first person plural is analytic in Ulster (cheannaíodh muid, not cheannaímis); the first person singular stays synthetic (cheannaínn). The standard form cheannaímis will be met in printed books and in the exam and should be recognised.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, briathra a thosaíonn ar f
rulesUlster.statement: A second-conjugation verb beginning with f takes d' as well as lenition in the positive: D'fhiosraíodh sé, D'fholmhaíodh sé. In the negative the d' is dropped and only the lenition remains: Ní fhiosraíodh sé. The question form eclipses: An bhfiosraíodh sé?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, briathra a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A verb beginning with a vowel takes d' in the positive (D'athraíodh sé, D'oibrídís, D'ullmhaínn) but not after Ní or An: Ní ullmhaínn, Ní aimsínn, An ullmhaíteá?, An aimsíteá?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an fhoirm dhiúltach
rulesUlster.statement: The negative is formed with Ní followed by lenition and no d': Ní cheannaínn, Ní bhailínn, Ní fhiosraínn, Ní ullmhaínn.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an fhoirm cheisteach
rulesUlster.statement: The question is formed with An followed by eclipsis: An gceannaíteá?, An mbailíteá?, An bhfiosraíteá?; a vowel-initial verb takes no change after An: An ullmhaíteá?

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite, an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The saorbhriathar (autonomous form) of the habitual past ends in -aítí or -ítí, with lenition on a consonant and d' before a vowel or f: Cheannaítí, Bhailítí, D'ullmhaítí, D'aimsítí, D'fhiosraítí, D'fhoilsítí leabhair sa chló Ghaelach.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite agus an modh coinníollach: comparáid
rulesUlster.statement: The book sets the habitual past beside the conditional to show that the personal endings match while the stem differs: the habitual past keeps the -aí-/-í- stem (Cheannaínn, Bhailínn, Cheannaíodh muid) and the conditional uses -ó-/-eo- (Cheannóinn, Bhaileoinn, Cheannódh muid); both take lenition, d' before vowels and f, Ní in the negative and An with eclipsis in the question. In both tenses the first person plural is analytic with muid in Ulster.

rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an modh coinníollach: na foirmeacha
rulesUlster.statement: The eleven irregular verbs have their own conditional stems, shown in the tables: bhéarfadh (beir), chloisfeadh (clois), thiocfadh (tar), d'íosfadh (ith), thabharfadh (tabhair), dhéanfadh (déan), d'fheicfeadh (feic), déarfadh (abair), rachadh (téigh), gheobhadh (faigh) and bheadh (bí). The section opens with a story in which each of these is used once in bold.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach: an fhoirm dhearfach (séimhiú agus d')
rulesUlster.statement: In the positive, the conditional stem is lenited where it can be (thabharfadh, dhéanfadh, chloisfeadh, thiocfadh, bhéarfadh, bheadh) and takes d' before a vowel or fh (d'íosfadh, d'fheicfeadh). Rachadh, déarfadh and gheobhadh are already in their fixed conditional shape and take no further change.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach: na deirí pearsanta
rulesUlster.statement: The personal endings are the same as for regular verbs: -(f)ainn (mé), -(f)á (tú), -(f)adh sé/sí, -(f)adh muid, -(f)adh sibh, -(f)aidís (siad), plus the saorbhriathar in -(f)aí or -(f)í. In Ulster the first person plural is analytic: bhéarfadh muid, rachadh muid, bheadh muid, gheobhadh muid, where the book prints bhéarfaimis, rachaimis, bheimis, gheobhaimis. The first person singular stays synthetic: bheinn, rachainn, d'íosfainn. The third person plural -(f)aidís is kept as in the book; pupils will also hear bheadh siad, rachadh siad in Donegal, and both are acceptable.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach: an fhoirm dhiúltach (Ní)
rulesUlster.statement: The negative is formed with Ní and lenition: Ní bhéarfadh, Ní chloisfeadh, Ní thiocfadh, Ní thabharfadh, Ní dhéanfadh, Ní fheicfeadh, Ní bheadh. Ní íosfadh and Ní déarfadh (and Ní rachadh) have no lenition, and faigh is the odd one out with eclipsis: Ní bhfaigheadh, Ní bhfaighinn, Ní bhfaighfí. The app uses Ní throughout; the local Cha is not taught.

rulesUlster.point: an modh coinníollach: an fhoirm cheisteach (An)
rulesUlster.statement: The question is formed with An and eclipsis: An mbéarfadh, An gcloisfeadh, An dtiocfadh, An íosfadh, An dtabharfadh, An ndéanfadh, An bhfeicfeadh, An ndéarfadh, An rachadh, An bhfaigheadh, An mbeadh. The answer repeats the verb with its pronoun, positive or negative: Rachadh sé. Ní rachadh sé.

rulesUlster.point: dá agus an modh coinníollach
rulesUlster.statement: The if-clause uses dá followed by eclipsis and the conditional: dá mbeadh, dá gcuirfinn, dá bhfaigheadh, dá mbeadh muid, dá mbeidís, dá rachaidís. Both halves of a conditional sentence are in the conditional mood: Dá mbeadh deich míle punt ag Pól, thabharfadh sé cuid de dá thuismitheoirí.

rulesUlster.point: an saorbhriathar sa mhodh coinníollach
rulesUlster.statement: The autonomous form ends in -faí or -fí and has no subject: Thabharfaí cuidiú dóibh dá mbeidís i gcruachás. Positive forms keep the lenition and d' (D'íosfaí, D'fheicfí, Bhéarfaí, Chloisfí, Thiocfaí, Dhéanfaí, Bheifí); Rachfaí, Déarfaí and Gheofaí are fixed. Negative: Ní bhéarfaí, Ní chloisfí, Ní íosfaí, Ní bhfaighfí, Ní bheifí. Question: An mbéarfaí?, An gcloisfí?, An bhfaighfí?, An mbeifí? (The book's example has cúnamh; the app uses the Ulster word cuidiú.)

rulesUlster.point: na focail cheiste sa mhodh coinníollach (Uladh)
rulesUlster.statement: The book's question words are replaced by the Ulster ones in every exercise: Céard a dhéanfá? becomes Cad é a dhéanfá?; Cathain a déarfadh duine? becomes Cá huair a déarfadh duine?; Cá rachfá? and Cá bhfaighfeá? become Cá háit a rachfá? and Cá háit a bhfaighfeá? (the a before the verb keeps the eclipsis). Cén teanga a chloisfeá? is the same in Ulster.

rulesUlster.point: nóta don eagarthóir: botúin chló sa leabhar
rulesUlster.statement: Several forms are misprinted in the book's tables and should not reach a pupil as printed (confirmed against the page images). Page 96: 'Tabharfá' (tabhair) should be Thabharfá; 'Ní rachfainn' (téigh) should be Ní rachainn; 'Bheifea' (bí) should be Bheifeá. Page 95: the Beir table is headed 'Béir' and prints 'Bhearfainn' without the fada (Bhéarfainn); the Clois table prints 'Chloisfidí' for Chloisfidís. All of these are silently corrected in the tables below. Smaller slips in the exercises: page 93 'púnt' (punt); page 94 B2 'ag teastail' (teastáil); page 95 E1 'go leir' (go léir) and item 5 'ar súil' (ar siúl). In Ceist item 5 (page 93) the question says 'sé' but the answers say 'sí'; the Ulster version below uses sí in both, since the sentence is about a gúna for a wedding, and the principal should confirm.

rulesUlster.point: nóta don eagarthóir: foirmeacha Uladh sa mhodh coinníollach
rulesUlster.statement: For sign-off: the book uses the standard conditional of feic (d'fheicfeadh sé, d'fheicfinn, d'fheicfí). In Ulster the positive independent forms are also tchífeadh sé, tchífinn, tchífí. Note that tchí is only the independent (positive) stem: after Ní, An, nach, go and dá the dependent stem feic is used in Ulster exactly as in the standard (Tchífeadh sé, but An bhfeicfeadh sé? and Ní fheicfeadh sé; Tchífinn, but Ní fheicfinn and An bhfeicfinn). So the only question for the principal is whether the positive tchífeadh / tchífinn / tchífí should replace d'fheicfeadh / d'fheicfinn / d'fheicfí; the negative and question forms stay as printed either way. The sentences below keep the book's standard d'fheicfeadh, as the house rule lists only the present tense tchí; every positive feic sentence is flagged. Two other Ulster vocabulary choices made below and worth a glance: de dhíth (for ag teastáil) and cuidiú (for cabhrú, cúnamh); i ndiaidh tamaill (for tar éis tamaill); achan lá, achan duine (for gach lá, gach éinne); gan airgead ar bith (for gan aon airgead). The book's gardaí is left in the two sentences about police, since it is the Irish word and not a dialect matter; the fresh sentences use póilíní for the school's own setting.
