rulesUlster.point: na briathra neamhrialta, an aimsir ghnáthchaite: an fhoirm dhearfach
rulesUlster.statement: The habitual past of the eleven irregular verbs is formed on the same stems as their present tense (téigh: théadh, tar: thagadh, tabhair: thugadh, feic: d'fheiceadh, clois: chloiseadh, faigh: d'fhaigheadh, ith: d'itheadh, beir: bheireadh, déan: dhéanadh, abair: deireadh, bí: bhíodh). The initial consonant is lenited and d' is prefixed to a vowel or to fh, exactly as with regular verbs. Ulster usage is the same; the school keeps d'fheiceadh rather than the more local tchíodh.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite: na foirceanna pearsanta
rulesUlster.statement: The endings are the same as for regular verbs: -inn (mé), -tá/-teá (tú: thagtá, thugtá, dhéantá after a broad stem; chloisteá, bhíteá, d'fheicteá after a slender stem), -adh/-eadh sé/sí, -adh/-eadh sibh, -aidís/-idís (siad), with the saorbhriathar in -taí/-tí. For the first person plural Ulster uses the analytic form with muid, théadh muid, chloiseadh muid, bhíodh muid, in place of the book's synthetic théimis, chloisimis, bhímis. The first person singular stays synthetic: théinn, bhínn, d'fhaighinn. The book gives the full paradigm for each irregular verb on pages 99 and 100.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite: an fhoirm dhiúltach agus cheisteach
rulesUlster.statement: The negative is formed with ní plus lenition (ní théadh sé, ní bhíodh sé) and the question with an plus eclipsis (an dtéadh sé?, an mbíodh sé?). Verbs beginning with a vowel take nothing after ní and nothing after an (ní itheadh sé, an itheadh sé?); after ní the d' is dropped and an fh- verb shows the lenited form (ní fheiceadh sé, ní fhaigheadh sé). Abair does not lenite after ní: ní deireadh sé. Note that faigh takes ní fhaigheadh in the habitual past; the eclipsed ní bhfaigheadh belongs to the conditional only.

rulesUlster.point: an aimsir ghnáthchaite: an saorbhriathar
rulesUlster.statement: The saorbhriathar of the habitual past ends in -tí or -taí (chloistí, d'ití, d'fheictí, thugtaí, d'fhaightí, deirtí, bhítí, thagtaí, dhéantaí, théití, bheirtí), with the same initial lenition or d' as the personal forms. Negative: ní chloistí; question: an gcloistí? Ulster usage is the same.

rulesUlster.point: nótaí eagarthóireachta: earráidí cló sa leabhar (le seiceáil ag an phríomhoide)
rulesUlster.statement: The printed tables contain several misprints that should not go to pupils as they stand: the Beir row is printed with a fada (Bhéirinn, Bhéiriteá, and so on) where the standard is bheirinn, bheirteá, and its negative is printed 'Ní bhéinn' for 'Ní bheirinn'; the Abair row is printed as 'Déirin' (for deirinn) and with a fada throughout (Déirteá, Déireadh, Déirtí) where the standard is deirinn, deirteá, deireadh, deirtí (the story on page 97 also prints 'Déireadh sé' while question 11 has the standard 'Deireadh sé'); the Téigh row prints 'Thiteá' for 'Théiteá'; the Feic row prints 'Ar bhfeictí?' for 'An bhfeictí?' and omits 'sé/sí' after 'D'fheiceadh'. Exercise B item 5 prints 'sa sú' (confirmed on the page image), an older spelling of 'sa zú'. The extracted answer to Exercise A item 9, 'Ní bhfaigheadh daoine cabhair ón stát', does not match the book's own table; the habitual past negative is 'Ní fhaigheadh', and that is what the paradigms below use.

rulesUlster.point: nóta Uladh: foirmeacha táite an iolra
rulesUlster.statement: The book's first person plural forms (théimis, chloisimis, thagaimis, dhéanaimis, bhímis and so on) and the exercise C items built on them are standard synthetic forms; in the app's Ulster usage these become analytic with muid (théadh muid, chloiseadh muid, ní thagadh muid), and the marker (Clois:sinn) in the stems becomes (Clois:muid). The first person singular synthetic forms (théinn, bhínn, d'fhaighinn) are kept. Elsewhere in this section the only Ulster changes are lexical (achan for gach, i ndiaidh for tar éis) and lenition after a simple preposition and the article (ag an cheoltóir).

rulesUlster.point: na réamhfhocail shimplí, an liosta
rulesUlster.statement: The simple prepositions covered are ar, ag, as, roimh, thar, idir, chuig, gan, faoi, le, do, de, ó, trí and i.

rulesUlster.point: réamhfhocal agus an t-alt 'an'
rulesUlster.statement: Some prepositions fuse with the singular article an: faoi + an gives faoin, le + an gives leis an, do + an gives don, de + an gives den, ó + an gives ón, trí + an gives tríd an, i + an gives sa. Before a vowel or fh, sa becomes san (san fhómhar, san oíche, san áit). The rest simply stand before it: ar an, ag an, as an, roimh an, thar an, idir an, chuig an, gan an.

rulesUlster.point: réamhfhocal agus an t-alt 'na'
rulesUlster.statement: Before the plural article na the prepositions are ar na, ag na, as na, roimh na, thar na, idir na, chuig na, gan na, faoi na, leis na, do na, de na, ó na, tríd na, and i + na gives sna.

rulesUlster.point: séimhiú i ndiaidh réamhfhocail shimplí
rulesUlster.statement: Lenition follows these simple prepositions when there is no article: ar, roimh, thar, faoi, do, de, gan, idir, ó, trí (trí bhalla, trí Ghaeilge). The less common preposition um also lenites (um Cháisc).

rulesUlster.point: urú i ndiaidh 'i'
rulesUlster.statement: Eclipsis follows the preposition i (i bpáirc, i gcruachás), but before a vowel it becomes in with no change to the noun (in Éirinn).

rulesUlster.point: ar an, ar na: consain
rulesUlster.statement: In Ulster, after ar an (and after every simple preposition plus the singular article) initial b, c, f, g, m and p are lenited, not eclipsed: ar an bhord, ar an chailín, ar an fhuinneog, ar an gheata, ar an pháirc. After ar na no change is made to any consonant, whether b, c, f, g, p or d, n, t, l, s (ar na buachaillí, ar na cailíní, ar na fuinneoga, ar na geataí, ar na páirceanna).

rulesUlster.point: ar an, ar na: gutaí
rulesUlster.statement: After ar an a vowel-initial noun is unchanged (ar an asal, ar an éan, ar an iascaire, ar an oráiste, ar an úll). After ar na, h is prefixed to a vowel (ar na hasail, ar na héin, ar na hiascairí, ar na horáistí, ar na húlla).

rulesUlster.point: ar an: d, n, t, l, s gan athrú
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns beginning with d, n, t, l or s take no change after ar an: ar an trá, ar an líne, ar an nuachtán, ar an droichead, ar an sagart. Exception: a feminine noun beginning with s followed by a vowel or l, n, r takes t before the s (ar an tsráid, ar an tsúil). Many Ulster speakers put t before masculine s-nouns as well (ar an tsagart); the app keeps the standard form for masculine nouns.

rulesUlster.point: 'ar' le mothúcháin agus staid
rulesUlster.statement: The preposition ar is used with words for feelings and states such as áthas, brón, fearg, eagla, imní, gliondar, díomá, ionadh, faitíos, náire, lúcháir, áiféala, uaigneas, scanradh, tuirse, ocras, amhras, bród, leisce, tart and éad: Tá ocras orthu, Tá tuirse air, Tá lúcháir uirthi. In Ulster lúcháir is the everyday word for áthas, and both are understood.

rulesUlster.point: 'ar' gan séimhiú i bhfrásaí seasta
rulesUlster.statement: Lenition is not applied after ar in set phrases such as ar saoire, ar meisce, ar crochadh, ar buile, ar cairde, ar ceal, ar crith, ar díol, ar fáil, ar fónamh, ar mire, ar seachrán, ar siúl, ar iarraidh, ar iasacht, ar oscailt, ar lorg.

rulesUlster.point: do, don: uatha
rulesUlster.statement: Lenition follows do (do Phól, do Mháire) and don (don bhuachaill, don chailín, don fhile, don ghirseach, don pháiste), except that nouns beginning with d, n, t, l, s or r are unchanged after don (don sagart, don tiománaí), and a vowel-initial noun takes no change after don (don aisteoir, don oibrí). Exception: a feminine noun beginning with s followed by a vowel or l, n, r takes t before the s (don tsráid, don tseanbhean).

rulesUlster.point: do na: iolra
rulesUlster.statement: After do na a consonant-initial noun is unchanged (do na páistí, do na gardaí, do na múinteoirí) and h is prefixed to a vowel (do na huain, do na héin, do na haisteoirí, do na hainmhithe).

rulesUlster.point: ag, ag an, ag na
rulesUlster.statement: No change follows ag on its own (ag Úna, ag Siobhán). In Ulster, after ag an, initial b, c, f, g, m and p are lenited (ag an bhuachaill, ag an chailín, ag an fháinleog, ag an gheata, ag an phíolóta) and a vowel is unchanged (ag an aisteoir, ag an éan, ag an iascaire, ag an othar, ag an uan). After ag na a consonant is unchanged (ag na buachaillí, ag na cailíní, ag na fáinleoga, ag na geataí, ag na píolótaí) and h is prefixed to a vowel (ag na hainmhithe, ag na héin, ag na hiascairí, ag na hothair, ag na huain).

rulesUlster.point: ag an: d, n, t, l, s gan athrú
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns beginning with d, t, l, s or n take no change after ag an: ag an doras, ag an tarracóir, ag an lampa, ag an siopa, ag an nead. Exception: a feminine noun beginning with s followed by a vowel or l, n, r takes t before the s (ag an tsráid, ag an tseanbhean). Many Ulster speakers put t before masculine s-nouns as well (ag an tsiopa); the app keeps the standard form for masculine nouns.

rulesUlster.point: an forainm réamhfhoclach
rulesUlster.statement: Each simple preposition combines with the personal pronouns to make a prepositional pronoun (ar + mé gives orm, do + mé gives dom, ag + mé gives agam, and so on); idir has plural forms only (eadrainn, eadraibh, eatarthu).

rulesUlster.point: réamhfhocail le briathra, riail ghinearálta
rulesUlster.statement: Certain verbs are always followed by a particular simple preposition, and the pupil must learn which preposition goes with which verb. The book teaches this by grouping verbs under seven prepositions: ar, de, le, do, chuig, ó and as.

rulesUlster.point: forainmneacha réamhfhoclacha
rulesUlster.statement: When one of these prepositions is followed by a personal pronoun (mé, tú, é, í, sinn, sibh, iad), the two fuse into a single prepositional pronoun, for example ar + mé becomes orm. Each preposition has its own table of seven forms, given as a Dul siar (revision) box. The forms are the same in Ulster usage.

rulesUlster.point: briathra + ar
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs that take ar include cuir (ar: put on, of clothing), beir (ar: catch), amharc (ar: look at; the book's féach ar is understood but Ulster says amharc ar) and teip (ar: fail, the person failing is the object of ar). Further examples: cnag ar, scairt ar (call to, the usual Ulster verb where the book also gives glaoigh ar), tosaigh ar, iarr ar (the person asked), crom ar, cuimhnigh ar, cuir isteach ar. After ar and the singular article, Ulster lenites: ar an bhord, ar an fhón.

rulesUlster.point: briathra + de
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs that take de include fiafraigh de (ask a question of someone), bain de (take off, of clothing), tit de (fall off) and tóg de (lift off). Further examples: lean de (continue with) and stad de (stop). Before the article de becomes den, which lenites: den bhean, den dréimire, den urlár.

rulesUlster.point: briathra + le
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs that take le include éist le (listen to), cabhraigh le (help; Ulster also says cuidigh le), buail le (meet) and díol le (sell to). Further examples: éirigh le (succeed), tig le (be able; the Ulster form), taitin le (please, be enjoyed by) and abair le (tell someone). After le and the singular article, Ulster lenites rather than eclipses: leis an bhean, leis an mhúinteoir. Before s the article gives t: leis an tseanbhean.

rulesUlster.point: briathra + do
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs that take do include tabhair do (give to), inis do (tell to) and taispeáin do (show to). Further examples: geall do (promise), lig do (allow), mol do (advise), tar do (suit, of clothes; Ulster also says fóir do) and beannaigh do (greet). Before the article do becomes don, which lenites: don chailín, don ghirseach.

rulesUlster.point: briathra + chuig
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs that take chuig (towards, to a person) include scríobh chuig (write to) and caith chuig (throw to). After chuig and the singular article, Ulster lenites: chuig an mhadadh, chuig an phríomhoide.

rulesUlster.point: briathra + ó
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs that take ó (from) include faigh ó (get from) and teastaigh ó (be needed or wanted by; the person wanting is the object of ó). Ó lenites a following noun: ó Mháire, ó Sheán. Before the article ó becomes ón, which lenites: ón bhaile, ón scoil.

rulesUlster.point: briathra + as
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs that take as include íoc as (pay for), díol as (also pay for: díol means both sell and pay, and in Donegal Irish díol is the ordinary verb for pay, so dhíol mé as means I paid for it) and éirigh as (give up). The book's heading here reads Briathar + as in the singular. After as and the singular article, Ulster lenites: as an bhaile, as an charr.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht: na dóigheanna lena húsáid
rulesUlster.statement: An adjective can be used in three ways: after the verb tá as a predicate (Tá sé tuirseach), in a copula exclamation of the shape Is + adjective + an + noun + é (Is deas an rothar é), or directly after the noun it describes (bean bhocht, asal beag dubh).

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht i ndiaidh ainmfhocail bhaininscnigh: séimhiú
rulesUlster.statement: When the adjective follows a feminine singular noun it is lenited (bean bhocht, girseach bheag); after a masculine noun it is not (asal beag dubh, gasúr beag). This also holds after a preposition and the article, where Ulster lenites the noun as well: ar an bhean chráifeach (the book's standard form is ar an mbean chráifeach). It matters for the gap exercises (an bhean chráifeach, obair shealadach, ócáid bhliantúil, áit fhothainiúil).

rulesUlster.point: céimeanna comparáide: breischéim agus sárchéim
rulesUlster.statement: The comparative is formed with níos plus the comparative form of the adjective (Tá Séamas níos airde) and the superlative with is plus the same form (Is é Tomás an duine is airde). The comparative form is the same in both degrees.

rulesUlster.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí a chríochnaíonn ar chonsan leathan
rulesUlster.statement: For a plain adjective ending in a broad consonant, slenderise the final consonant and add -e: ard becomes airde. Other examples given: bán, bocht, bog, caol, dearg, fuar, glas (báine, boichte, boige, caoile, deirge, fuaire, glaise).

rulesUlster.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -ach agus -each
rulesUlster.statement: An adjective ending in -ach changes -ach to -aí, and one ending in -each changes -each to -í: feargach becomes feargaí, díreach becomes dírí.

rulesUlster.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -úil
rulesUlster.statement: An adjective ending in -úil adds -a: éirimiúil becomes éirimiúla, cairdiúil becomes cairdiúla.

rulesUlster.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí ar -mhar agus -ar
rulesUlster.statement: An adjective ending in -mhar (or -ar) adds -e with slenderisation: luachmhar becomes luachmhaire, lúfar becomes lúfaire.

rulesUlster.point: breischéim: aidiachtaí a gcailltear guta iontu (coimriú)
rulesUlster.statement: Some two-syllable adjectives drop the vowel of the last syllable and add -e: ramhar becomes raimhre. The same type: folamh, daingean, íseal, uasal, álainn, domhain, saibhir, deacair, aoibhinn (foilmhe, daingne, ísle, uaisle, áille, doimhne, saibhre, deacra, aoibhne). The page image confirms the book prints domhan (the noun for world); the adjective meaning deep is domhain, and the app should use domhain. Ulster usage is the same as the standard here.

rulesUlster.point: comparáid chothrom: chomh ... le
rulesUlster.statement: To say as ... as, use chomh with the basic form of the adjective, not the comparative form, followed by le (Níl Muiris chomh fiosrach le Liam) or by is a (Níl sé chomh ceomhar anocht is a bhí sé aréir). Note that le followed by the article lenites in Ulster: chomh ceanúil leis an mhadadh.

rulesUlster.point: breischéim: níos ... ná, i bhfad níos
rulesUlster.statement: The thing compared is introduced with ná (Tá an áit seo níos contúirtí ná an áit eile), and i bhfad before níos strengthens the comparison (Tá ola i bhfad níos flúirsí anois). In Ulster níos is used in past-tense sentences too (Bhí an leabhar eile níos greannmhaire), so the book's practice suits the school and ní ba need not be taught.

rulesUlster.point: aidiachtaí a bhfuil breischéim ar leith acu
rulesUlster.statement: A small group of common adjectives has an irregular comparative form that must be learnt: maith, níos fearr; olc, níos measa; mór, níos mó; beag, níos lú; fada, níos faide; furast, níos fusa; te, níos teo; tréan, níos treise or níos tréine; breá, níos breátha. The same form follows is in the superlative. Furast is the Ulster spelling the book already uses (standard furasta).

forms: bán, bocht, bog, caol, dearg, fuar, glas.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, iolraí laga: caolú
rulesUlster.statement: Most weak plurals in the first declension are formed simply by making the final consonant of the word slender, for example bád becomes báid.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, iolraí laga: -a a chur leis
rulesUlster.statement: Some first-declension plurals are formed by adding -a to the word, for example ceart becomes cearta.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, tréaniolraí
rulesUlster.statement: Some words in this group have strong plurals, for example dán becomes dánta and cogadh becomes cogaí.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, inscne
rulesUlster.statement: All first-declension nouns are masculine.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, deireadh an fhocail
rulesUlster.statement: First-declension nouns end in a broad consonant.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha
rulesUlster.statement: The nominative singular is made slender to form the genitive singular, and the noun is lenited after the article where possible, for example an capall gives cosa an chapaill. This is the same in Ulster: the genitive singular after an lenites b, c, f, g, m and p, and leaves d and t alone (adharca an tairbh, dath an dorais).

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach iolra
rulesUlster.statement: The genitive plural has the same form as the nominative singular, and after na it is eclipsed where possible, for example seolta na mbád, cosa na gcapall (the book shows this in its examples rather than stating it). Ulster does not differ here: eclipsis after na in the genitive plural is standard everywhere.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns beginning with a vowel take t- in the nominative singular (an t-úll), nothing in the genitive singular (dath an úill), h in the nominative plural (na húlla, na hoileáin) and n- in the genitive plural (dath na n-úll, muintir na n-oileán).

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a thosaíonn ar s + guta
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns beginning with s followed by a vowel take t before the s in the genitive singular after the article (cóta an tsagairt, doras an tséipéil) but are unchanged in the genitive plural (cótaí na sagart, doirse na séipéal).

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, focail a chríochnaíonn ar -ach, -each
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns ending in -ach or -each change that ending to -aigh or -igh in the genitive singular and the nominative plural (an marcach, cáipín an mharcaigh, na marcaigh), while the genitive plural keeps the -ach form with eclipsis (cáipíní na marcach, oifigí na gcléireach).

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn ea go i
rulesUlster.statement: When the noun has ea before the final consonant, ea changes to i in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an fear, teach an fhir, na fir, tithe na bhfear.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn éa go éi
rulesUlster.statement: When the noun has éa before the final consonant, éa changes to éi in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an páipéar, dath an pháipéir, na páipéir, dath na bpáipéar. The book's box heading reads ÉA to Í, but every example shows éa becoming éi.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn íoch go igh
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns ending in -íoch change that ending to -igh in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an beithíoch, luach an bheithígh, na beithígh, luach na mbeithíoch. Beithíoch is a common Ulster word for an animal or beast (in Donegal often a horse), so pupils will meet it often.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, athraíonn ia go éi
rulesUlster.statement: When the noun has ia before the final consonant, ia changes to éi in the genitive singular and the nominative plural, for example an t-iasc, praghas an éisc, na héisc, praghas na n-iasc.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -í
rulesUlster.statement: The plural of a second declension noun can be formed by adding -í to the word, as in oifig, oifigí.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -anna, -eanna
rulesUlster.statement: The plural can be formed by adding -anna or -eanna to the word, as in scoil, scoileanna and ceist, ceisteanna. (The book's own examples under this heading, craobhacha and foirmeacha, actually show -acha and -eacha.)

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -a
rulesUlster.statement: The plural can be formed by adding -a to the word, as in amharclann, amharclanna.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -acha
rulesUlster.statement: The plural can be formed by adding -acha to the word, as in craobh, craobhacha.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tréithe ginearálta
rulesUlster.statement: Most of the nouns in this group are feminine, and they end in a consonant.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: an t-alt
rulesUlster.statement: In the genitive singular the article an changes to na, and the noun is not lenited after it: an fháinleog becomes sciathán na fáinleoige. This is the same in Ulster.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: -e
rulesUlster.statement: The commonest way of forming the genitive singular is to add -e to the noun, as in an scoil, doras na scoile.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: -each go -í
rulesUlster.statement: A noun ending in -each changes that ending to -í in the genitive singular, as in an ghirseach, cóta na girsí. Girseach is the everyday Ulster word for a girl, so this example suits the school well.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha: caolú agus -e
rulesUlster.statement: A noun ending in a broad consonant is slenderised and takes -e in the genitive singular, as in an phictiúrlann, clár na pictiúrlainne.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach: focail a thosaíonn ar ghuta
rulesUlster.statement: A noun beginning with a vowel takes h after na in the genitive singular and n- after na in the genitive plural: an oifig, doras na hoifige, doirse na n-oifigí.

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, rialacha caolaithe
rulesUlster.statement: When the noun is slenderised for the genitive singular, ea becomes i in words of more than one syllable (doineann, doininne), ea becomes ei in others (speach, speiche), with cearc, circe as an exception, and ia becomes éi (grian, gréine).

rulesUlster.point: an dara díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach iolra
rulesUlster.statement: In the genitive plural the article na eclipses a following consonant and puts n- before a vowel, and nouns whose plural ends in -a lose that ending (na bróga, dath na mbróg) while nouns whose plural ends in -anna, -eanna or -í keep it (na fadhbanna, tús na bhfadhbanna). Eclipsis after na in the genitive plural applies in Ulster exactly as in the standard; the Ulster lenition after a preposition and the article (ar an bhord) does not affect this.

rulesUlster.point: an tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rulesUlster.statement: A noun that is the object of a verbal noun goes into the genitive case, as in ag canadh amhráin, ag cur báistí (or, in Ulster, ag cur fearthainne), ag glanadh na fuinneoige. This is stated on page 141 for first declension nouns and repeated on page 149 for second declension nouns.

rulesUlster.point: an chéad díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach (athbhreithniú)
rulesUlster.statement: Pages 140 to 143 are revision exercises on the first declension genitive, singular and plural, with and without the article, and with personal names, before the second declension is introduced on page 144. In the sentence exercises the Ulster versions lenite after a simple preposition and the article (ar an bhord, ar an charr) instead of eclipsing.

paradigmsUlster.title: An Dara Díochlaonadh: Iolraí (cumtar an uimhir iolra)
forms: (i) Trí -í a chur leis an fhocal: Oifig, Oifigí
(ii) Trí -anna, -eanna a chur leis an fhocal: Scoil, Scoileanna; Ceist, Ceisteanna (the book prints Craobh, Craobhacha and Foirm, Foirmeacha here)
(iii) Trí -a a chur leis an fhocal: Amharclann, Amharclanna
(iv) Trí -acha a chur leis an fhocal: Craobh, Craobhacha

paradigmsUlster.title: Iolraí: pictiúir (uatha agus iolra)
An Dara Díochlaonadh: samplaí, uatha agus iolra, ainmneach agus ginideach
forms: 1 (-e): An scoil, na scoileanna; Doras na scoile, Doirse na scoileanna

2 (each > í): An ghirseach, na girseacha; Cóta na girsí, cótaí na ngirseach (the book prints cótaí na ngirseacha on page 146, which departs from its own rule that a plural in -a loses the ending in the genitive plural)

3 (caolú + e): An phictiúrlann, na pictiúrlanna; Clár na pictiúrlainne, cláracha na bpictiúrlann (the book prints na bpictiúrlanna on page 147; cláracha is the older and Ulster plural of clár, the standard plural being cláir, and is acceptable here)
4 (-e) Focail a thosaíonn ar ghuta: An oifig, na hoifigí; Doras na hoifige, doirse na n-oifigí

paradigmsUlster.title: Déantar caolú de réir na rialacha seo
forms: ea > ei: speach, speiche. Ach [cearc > circe]

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -anna
rulesUlster.statement: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -anna to the word: rang becomes ranganna.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -í
rulesUlster.statement: Most third-declension nouns, including the agent nouns in -éir, -eoir, -óir, -úir and abstract nouns in -acht and -int, form their plural by adding -í: cainteoir becomes cainteoirí, beannacht becomes beannachtaí, canúint becomes canúintí.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -acha
rulesUlster.statement: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -acha to the word: barúil becomes barúlacha.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra: -ta, -te
rulesUlster.statement: Some third-declension nouns form their plural by adding -ta or -te to the word: gleann becomes gleannta.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, inscne
rulesUlster.statement: The third declension contains both masculine and feminine nouns.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, deireadh an fhocail
rulesUlster.statement: Every noun in the third declension ends in a consonant.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: -a
rulesUlster.statement: The genitive singular is formed by adding -a to the word. If the final consonant is slender it is made broad first: éir becomes éara, eoir becomes eora, óir becomes óra, úir becomes úra.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: io go ea
rulesUlster.statement: In one-syllable words the vowel group io changes to ea in the genitive: sioc gives seaca (ag cur seaca), fios gives feasa (ag lorg feasa).

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: focail ar -int
rulesUlster.statement: In words ending in -int the t is dropped after broadening in the genitive: tuiscint becomes tuisceana.

rulesUlster.point: an tríú díochlaonadh, an tuiseal ginideach uatha: focail ar -irt
rulesUlster.statement: In words ending in -irt the t becomes tha after broadening in the genitive: buairt becomes buartha.

rulesUlster.point: an tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rulesUlster.statement: The genitive case follows a verbal noun: ag ól fíona, ag foghlaim an cheachta.

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tréaniolraí
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns of the fourth declension have strong plurals, and most of them end in -í, -te, -the or -anna in the plural.

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -í
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns ending in -ín in the singular, and most nouns ending in -a, -e or -aire, add í to form the plural (an siopa, na siopaí; an béile, na béilí; an cócaire, na cócairí).

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -te/-the
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns ending in -aí or -í, and a small group ending in -é or -e, add -te or -the in the plural (an t-ainmhí, na hainmhithe; an scéalaí, na scéalaithe; an ghné, na gnéithe; an líne, na línte; an tine, na tinte).

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -anna
rulesUlster.statement: Nouns ending in -o or -u, and some nouns ending in -a or -á, add -anna in the plural (an cú, na cúnna; an cnó, na cnónna; an trá, na tránna; an tua, na tuanna).

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolra -anna (focail eile)
rulesUlster.statement: A further group of nouns in this declension, mostly short loan words and words ending in -é, also take -anna in the plural (an bus, na busanna; an ghé, na géanna).

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, iolraí neamhrialta
rulesUlster.statement: Some fourth-declension nouns follow none of the patterns A to D and their plurals must be learned individually (an gabha, na gaibhne; an contae, na contaethe; an comhrá, na comhráite; an t-ainm, na hainmneacha; an oíche, na hoícheanta).

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, críoch na bhfocal
rulesUlster.statement: In the fourth declension almost every noun ends in -ín or in a vowel.

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, inscne
rulesUlster.statement: Most fourth-declension nouns are masculine, but there are feminine nouns in it too.

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha, firinscneach
rulesUlster.statement: In the genitive singular the noun itself does not change; after the article an, a masculine noun is lenited (teach an chailín, dath an bhosca) and t is normally prefixed to a noun beginning with s (fear an tsiopa). A vowel-initial noun takes no prefix (praghas an oráiste).

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach uatha, baininscneach
rulesUlster.statement: In the genitive singular of a feminine noun the article changes from an to na, and h is prefixed to a noun beginning with a vowel (tús na haiste, éide na banaltra, barr na sleá).

rulesUlster.point: an ceathrú díochlaonadh, tuiseal ginideach iolra
rulesUlster.statement: The genitive plural has the same form as the nominative plural, with na before it; the noun is eclipsed after na (tithe na gcailíní, dath na mboscaí, éidí na mbanaltraí) and n- is prefixed to a vowel (praghas na n-oráistí, tús na n-aistí).

rulesUlster.point: an tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rulesUlster.statement: A noun that follows a verbal noun (ag oscailt, ag scríobh) goes into the genitive: ag oscailt an fhéirín, ag scríobh na haiste. This is the same in Ulster; note that ag amharc ar (Ulster for ag féachaint ar) takes ar and so does not put the noun in the genitive.

paradigmsUlster.title: Iolra -í: samplaí (Ainmneach Uatha, Ainmneach Iolra)
Iolra -í: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -ín
forms: Báidín, bairín, báisín, builín, báinín, caipín, cipín, coinín, crúiscín, dreoilín, éinín, féirín, naipcín, nóinín, ribín, sabhaircín, sicín, toitín.

paradigmsUlster.title: Iolra -í: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -a
forms: Bata, bóna, bosca, cáca, cófra, dalta, garda, gúna, hata, mála, píopa, srl.

paradigmsUlster.title: Iolra -í: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -e
forms: Bairille, císte, cluiche, cnaipe, coiste, coláiste, file, oráiste, páiste, pointe, staighre, uisce, aiste, cuisle, gloine, táille, srl.

paradigmsUlster.title: Iolra -í: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -(a)ire
Iolra -te/-the: samplaí (Ainmneach Uatha, Ainmneach Iolra)
Iolra -te/-the: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -aí, ar -í, agus roinnt focal ar -é agus -e
forms: (-aí) Gréasaí, ceannaí, ceardaí, cleasaí, Críostaí, gadaí, moncaí
(-í) Ní, oibrí, dlí, rí, croí, slí
(-é, -e) Gné, líne, tine, tuile, féile (na gnéithe, na línte, na tinte, na tuilte, na féilte)

paradigmsUlster.title: Iolra -anna: samplaí (Ainmneach Uatha, Ainmneach Iolra)
Iolra -anna: focail a chríochnaíonn ar -o, -u, -a, -á
forms: Lao, ceo, brú, liú, tlú, bia, fia, nia, bua, bá, fleá, grua, íomhá, sleá, glao, rogha.

paradigmsUlster.title: Iolra -anna: focail eile (Ainmneach Uatha, Ainmneach Iolra)
Iolra -anna: focail eile
forms: Ceant, pas, seans, seic, snáithe, sraoth, stop, téacs, cé, cré, ré.

rulesUlster.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, inscne
rulesUlster.statement: Most nouns in the fifth declension are feminine.

rulesUlster.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, deireadh an ainmnigh uatha
rulesUlster.statement: Fifth-declension nouns end in -in, -il, -ir or in a vowel in the nominative singular (traein, abhainn, riail, triail, cathaoir, litir, uimhir, lacha, cara, comharsa).

rulesUlster.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, deireadh an ghinidigh uatha
rulesUlster.statement: In the genitive singular these nouns end in -ch, -n, -d or -r, which gives four main groups of nouns; Nollaig (genitive Nollag) is treated separately as a fifth group.

rulesUlster.point: an cúigiú díochlaonadh, an uimhir iolra
rulesUlster.statement: Most fifth-declension nouns form their plural in -(e)acha (traenacha, litreacha, cathaoireacha, mainistreacha, aithreacha); a small number are irregular and must be learned: bráithre, caoirigh, ingne, lachain, cairde, monarchana, comharsana, naimhde, nollaigí, tríochaidí.

rulesUlster.point: an ginideach uatha ar -(e)ach
rulesUlster.statement: Group A nouns add -(e)ach in the genitive singular: an chathaoir becomes na cathaoireach, an litir becomes na litreach, an eochair becomes na heochrach. Some drop a vowel (syncopate) before the ending: an chathair becomes na cathrach, an mhainistir becomes na mainistreach.

rulesUlster.point: an ginideach uatha ar -n
rulesUlster.statement: Group B nouns end in -n in the genitive singular: an abhainn becomes na habhann, an chomharsa becomes na comharsan, an teorainn becomes na teorann, an mhonarcha becomes na monarchan, an ionga becomes na hiongan, an lacha becomes na lachan.

rulesUlster.point: an ginideach uatha ar -d
rulesUlster.statement: Group C: cara ends in -d in the genitive singular, an cara becomes an charad (teach an charad).

rulesUlster.point: an ginideach uatha ar -r
rulesUlster.statement: Group D, the family words, end in -r in the genitive singular and drop the i of the last syllable: an t-athair becomes an athar, an deartháir becomes an dearthár, an bráthair becomes an bhráthar, an mháthair becomes na máthar, and an deirfiúr becomes na deirféar.

rulesUlster.point: an ginideach uatha, Nollaig
rulesUlster.statement: Group E: Nollaig has the genitive singular Nollag, tús na Nollag.

rulesUlster.point: an ginideach iolra
rulesUlster.statement: For nouns whose plural ends in -(e)acha or -e the genitive plural is the same as the nominative plural, with eclipsis after na (dath na gcathaoireacha, troime na n-eochracha, tithe na gcairde); but caoirigh, comharsana and lachain take the short genitive plural caorach, comharsan, lachan (cosa na gcaorach, gairdíní na gcomharsan, cleití na lachan).

rulesUlster.point: an ginideach i ndiaidh an ainm bhriathartha
rulesUlster.statement: A noun that follows a verbal noun goes into the genitive: ag casadh na heochrach, ag glanadh na monarchan.

paradigmsUlster.title: An Cúigiú Díochlaonadh: Uatha agus Iolra
A. Ainmfhocail a chríochnaíonn ar -(e)ach: Ainmneach uatha agus Ginideach uatha
B. Ainmfhocail a chríochnaíonn ar -n sa Ghinideach uatha: Ainmneach uatha agus Ginideach uatha
C. Ainmfhocail a chríochnaíonn ar -d sa Ghinideach uatha
D. Ainmfhocail a chríochnaíonn ar -r sa Ghinideach uatha
E. Nollaig: Ainmneach uatha agus Ginideach uatha
A. Ainmneach Iolra agus Ginideach Iolra (ainmfhocail ar -(e)ach)
B. Ainmneach Iolra agus Ginideach Iolra (ainmfhocail ar -n)
C. Ainmneach Iolra agus Ginideach Iolra (ainmfhocail ar -d)
D. Ainmneach Iolra agus Ginideach Iolra (ainmfhocail ar -r)

rulesUlster.point: réamhfhocail chomhshuite agus an tuiseal ginideach
rulesUlster.statement: A compound preposition (a simple preposition plus a noun, such as ar son, i measc, os comhair) is followed by the genitive case: the noun after it goes into the genitive, and the article becomes an (masculine), na (feminine) or na (plural) with the usual genitive mutations. Ulster usage is the same as the standard here: the lenition that Ulster uses after a simple preposition and the article (ar an bhord) does not apply after a compound preposition, because the noun is in the genitive (ar son an bhoird, ar son na tíre).

rulesUlster.point: na réamhfhocail chomhshuite is coitianta
rulesUlster.statement: The book gives a reference list of the commonest compound prepositions, grouped by their first element: ar (aghaidh, feadh, lorg, nós, son), os (cionn, coinne, comhair), i/in (bhfeighil, bhfogas, dteannta, gcaitheamh, gceann, gcoinne, gcuideachta, mbun, ndiaidh, rith, aghaidh, ionad, aice, éadan) and le (cois, haghaidh, hais, linn). Each of these takes the genitive. All of them are used in Ulster; pupils will also hear fá choinne (for, to get) beside le haghaidh, and it takes the genitive in the same way.

sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses bliain (bliana).

sentences.original: Rith na buachaillí ar nós (an ghaoth).
sentences.ulster: Rith na buachaillí ar nós na gaoithe.
sentences.fresh: Bhí sé ag ithe ar nós na muice.
sentences.stem: Bhí sé ag ithe ar nós (an mhuc).
sentences.point: ar nós + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 2ú díochlaonadh (an ghaoth: na gaoithe)
sentences.note: No Ulster change; buachaillí is kept, though gasúir would also be heard. Fresh stem uses muc (an mhuc: na muice), so the pupil must remove the lenition as well as change the article.

sentences.ulster: Sheas sé os comhair na fuinneoige.
sentences.fresh: Labhair an captaen os comhair na foirne.
sentences.stem: Labhair an captaen os comhair (an fhoireann).
sentences.point: os comhair + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 2ú díochlaonadh (an fhuinneog: na fuinneoige)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses foireann (an fhoireann: na foirne), which also removes the lenition.

sentences.original: Tá an fear sin i bhfeighil (an pháirc).
sentences.ulster: Tá an fear sin i bhfeighil na páirce.
sentences.fresh: Tá Bean Uí Néill i bhfeighil na leabharlainne.
sentences.stem: Tá Bean Uí Néill i bhfeighil (an leabharlann).
sentences.point: i bhfeighil + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 2ú díochlaonadh (an pháirc: na páirce)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses leabharlann (na leabharlainne); Bean Uí Néill is an invented name.

sentences.original: Bíonn sé i gcónaí i gcuideachta (na cailíní).
sentences.ulster: Bíonn sé i gcónaí i gcuideachta na gcailíní.
sentences.fresh: Bíonn sí i gcónaí i gcuideachta na ngasúr.
sentences.stem: Bíonn sí i gcónaí i gcuideachta (na gasúir).
sentences.point: i gcuideachta + tuiseal ginideach iolra, urú i ndiaidh na (na cailíní: na gcailíní)
sentences.note: No Ulster change to the book sentence. Fresh stem uses the Ulster gasúr (na gasúir: na ngasúr), a strong plural whose genitive plural is the same as the singular.

sentences.original: Tiocfaidh mé ar ais i gceann (coicís).
sentences.ulster: Tiocfaidh mé ar ais i gceann coicíse.
sentences.fresh: Beidh na scrúduithe ann i gceann seachtaine.
sentences.stem: Beidh na scrúduithe ann i gceann (seachtain).
sentences.point: i gceann + tuiseal ginideach, ainmfhocal baininscneach gan alt (coicís: coicíse)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses seachtain (seachtaine).

sentences.original: Thug sé cuairt orainn i ndiaidh (an tsochraid).
sentences.ulster: Thug sé cuairt orainn i ndiaidh na sochraide.
sentences.fresh: Bhí mé tuirseach i ndiaidh na seachtaine.
sentences.stem: Bhí mé tuirseach i ndiaidh (an tseachtain).
sentences.point: i ndiaidh + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 2ú díochlaonadh (an tsochraid: na sochraide)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses seachtain (an tseachtain: na seachtaine), so the pupil must drop the t before s.

sentences.original: Sheas na daoine os comhair (an altóir).
sentences.ulster: Sheas na daoine os comhair na haltóra.
sentences.fresh: Bhí muid inár suí os comhair na habhann.
sentences.stem: Bhí muid inár suí os comhair (an abhainn).
sentences.point: os comhair + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 5ú díochlaonadh, h roimh ghuta i ndiaidh na (an altóir: na haltóra)
sentences.note: No Ulster change to the book sentence. Fresh stem uses abhainn (na habhann), fifth declension feminine beginning with a vowel.

sentences.original: Rinne sí é i gcoinne mo (toil).
sentences.ulster: Rinne sí é i gcoinne mo thola.
sentences.fresh: Chuir mé an fón síos i gcoinne mo thola.
sentences.stem: Chuir mé an fón síos i gcoinne mo (toil).
sentences.point: i gcoinne + tuiseal ginideach i ndiaidh aidiacht shealbhach (mo thoil: mo thola)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. The fresh stem keeps toil because the point is the genitive of that fixed phrase after a possessive.

sentences.original: Bhí sé sa teach sin le haghaidh (na blianta).
sentences.ulster: Bhí sé sa teach sin le haghaidh na mblianta.
sentences.fresh: Bhí sí ag traenáil le haghaidh na gcluichí.
sentences.stem: Bhí sí ag traenáil le haghaidh (na cluichí).
sentences.point: le haghaidh + tuiseal ginideach iolra, urú i ndiaidh na (na blianta: na mblianta)
sentences.note: No Ulster change; t is unchanged after sa. Fresh stem uses cluichí (na gcluichí). Ulster pupils may also say fá choinne na gcluichí.

sentences.ulster: D'fhan sé i gcuideachta na dtincéirí.
sentences.fresh: D'fhan sé i gcuideachta na gceoltóirí.
sentences.stem: D'fhan sé i gcuideachta (na ceoltóirí).
sentences.point: i gcuideachta + tuiseal ginideach iolra, urú i ndiaidh na (na tincéirí: na dtincéirí)
sentences.note: Cultural change. The book's noun tincéirí is now regarded as a slur for Travellers and should not go before pupils; the Ulster version is given only as the faithful rendering of the book. The fresh stem uses ceoltóirí (na gceoltóirí) and tests the same eclipsis. Principal to confirm the original is withheld from the app.

sentences.ulster: Dhóigh siad gual in ionad móna.
sentences.fresh: D'ith mé toradh in ionad seacláide.
sentences.stem: D'ith mé toradh in ionad (seacláid).
sentences.point: in ionad + tuiseal ginideach, ainmfhocal baininscneach gan alt (móin: móna)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses seacláid (seacláide), feminine without the article.

sentences.original: Bhí na páistí ciúin le linn (an ceacht).
sentences.ulster: Bhí na páistí ciúin le linn an cheachta.
sentences.fresh: Bhí na fóin múchta le linn an cheachta.
sentences.stem: Bhí na fóin múchta le linn (an ceacht).
sentences.point: le linn + tuiseal ginideach, 3ú díochlaonadh firinscneach, séimhiú i ndiaidh an (an ceacht: an cheachta)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. The fresh stem keeps ceacht, the natural third declension noun for a classroom sentence, in a modern setting.

sentences.original: Bhí picnic acu in aice (an loch).
sentences.ulster: Bhí picnic acu in aice an locha.
sentences.fresh: Chuaigh muid ag siúl in aice an locha.
sentences.stem: Chuaigh muid ag siúl in aice (an loch).
sentences.point: in aice + tuiseal ginideach, 3ú díochlaonadh firinscneach (an loch: an locha)
sentences.note: No Ulster change to the book sentence. Fresh stem keeps loch (l cannot lenite) and uses the Ulster chuaigh muid.

sentences.original: Sheas an múinteoir os comhair (an rang).
sentences.ulster: Sheas an múinteoir os comhair an ranga.
sentences.fresh: Rinne Ciara a cur i láthair os comhair an ranga.
sentences.stem: Rinne Ciara a cur i láthair os comhair (an rang).
sentences.point: os comhair + tuiseal ginideach, 3ú díochlaonadh firinscneach (an rang: an ranga)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem keeps rang (r cannot lenite) in a new sentence.

sentences.original: Chuaigh siad isteach i ndiaidh (an sos).
sentences.ulster: Chuaigh siad isteach i ndiaidh an tsosa.
sentences.fresh: Bhí ocras orm i ndiaidh an tsnámha.
sentences.stem: Bhí ocras orm i ndiaidh (an snámh).
sentences.point: i ndiaidh + tuiseal ginideach, 3ú díochlaonadh firinscneach, t roimh s i ndiaidh an (an sos: an tsosa)
sentences.note: The book prints isteadh, a misprint for isteach. No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses snámh (an tsnámha).

sentences.ulster: Throid siad ar son na poblachta.
sentences.fresh: Labhair sí ar son na Gaeltachta.
sentences.stem: Labhair sí ar son (an Ghaeltacht).
sentences.point: ar son + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 3ú díochlaonadh (an phoblacht: na poblachta)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses Gaeltacht (an Ghaeltacht: na Gaeltachta), third declension feminine, and removes the lenition in the same way.

sentences.ulster: Cé atá i bhfeighil an choláiste?
sentences.fresh: Cé atá i bhfeighil an chlub?
sentences.stem: Cé atá i bhfeighil (an club)?
sentences.point: i bhfeighil + tuiseal ginideach, 4ú díochlaonadh firinscneach, séimhiú i ndiaidh an (an coláiste: an choláiste)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses club (an chlub), fourth declension masculine with lenition after an.

sentences.ulster: Rith sí i ndiaidh an ghadaí.
sentences.fresh: Rith mé i ndiaidh an bhus ar maidin ach chaill mé é.
sentences.stem: Rith mé i ndiaidh (an bus) ar maidin ach chaill mé é.
sentences.point: i ndiaidh + tuiseal ginideach, 4ú díochlaonadh firinscneach, séimhiú i ndiaidh an (an gadaí: an ghadaí)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses bus (an bhus) in a fuller pupil sentence, as the checker proposed.

sentences.original: Bhí glasraí acu ar chúl (an gairdín).
sentences.ulster: Bhí glasraí acu ar chúl an ghairdín.
sentences.fresh: Tá an carr páirceáilte ar chúl an gharáiste.
sentences.stem: Tá an carr páirceáilte ar chúl (an garáiste).
sentences.point: ar chúl + tuiseal ginideach, 4ú díochlaonadh firinscneach, séimhiú i ndiaidh an (an gairdín: an ghairdín)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses garáiste (an gharáiste).

sentences.original: Bhí mo dheirfiúr mór i bhfeighil (na páistí).
sentences.ulster: Bhí mo dheirfiúr mór i bhfeighil na bpáistí.
sentences.fresh: Bhí Seán i bhfeighil na mbuachaillí ar an turas scoile.
sentences.stem: Bhí Seán i bhfeighil (na buachaillí) ar an turas scoile.
sentences.point: i bhfeighil + tuiseal ginideach iolra, urú i ndiaidh na (na páistí: na bpáistí)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses buachaillí (na mbuachaillí).

sentences.original: Shuigh sé sa teach i gcaitheamh (an tráthnóna).
sentences.ulster: Shuigh sé sa teach i gcaitheamh an tráthnóna.
sentences.fresh: Bhí mé ar mo fhón i gcaitheamh an tráthnóna.
sentences.stem: Bhí mé ar mo fhón i gcaitheamh (an tráthnóna).
sentences.point: i gcaitheamh + tuiseal ginideach, 4ú díochlaonadh firinscneach, gan athrú ar an fhocal ná ar an alt (an tráthnóna: an tráthnóna)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. The fresh stem keeps tráthnóna because the point is that nothing changes after an with a fourth declension noun beginning with t. Point reworded as the checker proposed.

sentences.ulster: Throid siad ar son na fírinne.
sentences.fresh: Bhí na daoine ag máirseáil ar son na saoirse.
sentences.stem: Bhí na daoine ag máirseáil ar son (an tsaoirse).
sentences.point: ar son + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 4ú díochlaonadh (an fhírinne: na fírinne)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses saoirse (an tsaoirse: na saoirse), fourth declension feminine, in a different sentence; the pupil drops the t rather than the lenition.

sentences.ulster: Bhí sé in aice na trá.
sentences.fresh: Tá Cill Chaoil in aice na farraige.
sentences.stem: Tá Cill Chaoil in aice (an fharraige).
sentences.point: in aice + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 4ú díochlaonadh (an trá: na trá)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses farraige (an fharraige: na farraige); Cill Chaoil is Kilkeel.

sentences.original: Shuíomar le cois (an tine) san oíche.
sentences.ulster: Shuigh muid le cois na tine san oíche.
sentences.fresh: Shuigh muid le cois na tine sa Ghaeltacht i nDún na nGall.
sentences.stem: Shuigh muid le cois (an tine) sa Ghaeltacht i nDún na nGall.
sentences.point: le cois + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 4ú díochlaonadh (an tine: na tine); foirm scartha Uladh (shuigh muid) in ionad Shuíomar an leabhair
sentences.note: Verb changed: the synthetic Shuíomar becomes shuigh muid. Fresh stem keeps tine and the Ulster verb form. Flagged only so the principal confirms the analytic form is wanted in the answer key.

sentences.original: Bhí an t-arm ar diúité ar fud (an dúiche).
sentences.ulster: Bhí an t-arm ar diúité ar fud na dúiche.
sentences.fresh: Bhí bratacha Ard Mhacha ar fud na dúiche.
sentences.stem: Bhí bratacha Ard Mhacha ar fud (an dúiche).
sentences.point: ar fud + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 4ú díochlaonadh (an dúiche: na dúiche)
sentences.note: Cultural change. An army on duty across the district is not a sentence for a South Armagh classroom; the Ulster rendering is faithful to the book, but the fresh stem (county flags across the district) is the one to use. Principal to confirm the original is withheld.

sentences.original: Sheas an balla i gcoinne (an taoide).
sentences.ulster: Sheas an balla i gcoinne na taoide.
sentences.fresh: Vótáil an rang i gcoinne na comhairle.
sentences.stem: Vótáil an rang i gcoinne (an chomhairle).
sentences.point: i gcoinne + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 4ú díochlaonadh (an taoide: na taoide)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses comhairle (an chomhairle: na comhairle), fourth declension feminine.

sentences.original: Bíonn a lán daoine i lár (an chathair).
sentences.ulster: Bíonn a lán daoine i lár na cathrach.
sentences.fresh: Bhí sé ina shuí i lár na traenach.
sentences.stem: Bhí sé ina shuí i lár (an traein).
sentences.point: i lár + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 5ú díochlaonadh (an chathair: na cathrach)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses traein (na traenach), fifth declension feminine.

sentences.original: Chaith sé oíche ar lorg (an eochair).
sentences.ulster: Chaith sé oíche ar lorg na heochrach.
sentences.fresh: Chaith sí bomaite ar lorg na huimhreach.
sentences.stem: Chaith sí bomaite ar lorg (an uimhir).
sentences.point: ar lorg + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 5ú díochlaonadh, h roimh ghuta i ndiaidh na (an eochair: na heochrach)
sentences.note: No Ulster change to the book sentence. Fresh stem uses uimhir (na huimhreach) and the Ulster bomaite.

sentences.original: Bhí sí ag fanacht le haghaidh (an litir).
sentences.ulster: Bhí sí ag fanacht le haghaidh na litreach.
sentences.fresh: Cheannaigh sí stampa le haghaidh na litreach.
sentences.stem: Cheannaigh sí stampa le haghaidh (an litir).
sentences.point: le haghaidh + tuiseal ginideach baininscneach, 5ú díochlaonadh (an litir: na litreach)
sentences.note: No Ulster change to the book sentence; the book's le haghaidh is kept because it is the point. Fresh stem, as the checker proposed, uses le haghaidh in a purpose sense (buying a stamp for the letter), which is natural in Ulster, and still tests litir (na litreach). Ulster pupils may also say fá choinne na litreach.

sentences.ulster: Bhí sí ar nós máthar.
sentences.fresh: Bhí sé ar nós athar dúinn.
sentences.stem: Bhí sé ar nós (athair) dúinn.
sentences.point: ar nós + tuiseal ginideach, 5ú díochlaonadh gan alt (máthair: máthar)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem uses athair (athar), fifth declension without the article.

sentences.original: Bhí sé anseo i rith (an lá).
sentences.ulster: Bhí sé anseo i rith an lae.
sentences.fresh: Bhí an ghrian ag taitneamh i rith an lae.
sentences.stem: Bhí an ghrian ag taitneamh i rith (an lá).
sentences.point: i rith + tuiseal ginideach, ainmfhocal neamhrialta (an lá: an lae)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem keeps the irregular lá (an lae); reworded as the checker proposed to avoid repeating the opening of the le linn an cheachta sentence.

sentences.ulster: Fágadh mise i mbun an tí.
sentences.fresh: Fágadh Laoise i mbun an tí nuair a bhí a tuismitheoirí amuigh.
sentences.stem: Fágadh Laoise i mbun (an teach) nuair a bhí a tuismitheoirí amuigh.
sentences.point: i mbun + tuiseal ginideach, ainmfhocal neamhrialta (an teach: an tí)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem keeps the irregular teach (an tí); Laoise is an invented name.

sentences.ulster: Rinne sé é ar son Dé.
sentences.fresh: Rinne siad an obair sin ar son Dé.
sentences.stem: Rinne siad an obair sin ar son (Dia).
sentences.point: ar son + tuiseal ginideach, ainmfhocal neamhrialta (Dia: Dé)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem keeps Dia (Dé) because the irregular genitive is the point.

sentences.ulster: Beidh sé anseo i gceann míosa.
sentences.fresh: Beidh an Nollaig ann i gceann míosa.
sentences.stem: Beidh an Nollaig ann i gceann (mí).
sentences.point: i gceann + tuiseal ginideach, ainmfhocal neamhrialta (mí: míosa)
sentences.note: No Ulster change. Fresh stem keeps mí (míosa); reworded as the checker proposed so it no longer duplicates the i gceann seachtaine sentence.

sentences.ulster: Chuaigh sé ann ar lorg dí.
sentences.fresh: Chuaigh sé isteach sa siopa ar lorg dí.
sentences.stem: Chuaigh sé isteach sa siopa ar lorg (deoch).
sentences.point: ar lorg + tuiseal ginideach, ainmfhocal neamhrialta (deoch: dí)
sentences.note: No Ulster change; s is unchanged after sa. Fresh stem keeps deoch (dí).

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha le 'ag' (Tá sé ag canadh)
rulesUlster.statement: The verbal noun is used after 'ag' with the verb 'bí' to say what someone is doing now: Tá sé ag canadh, Tá sí ag scuabadh, Tá siad ag obair. Pages 178 to 181 teach this through photograph captions only. The question that goes with it in Ulster is 'Cad é atá ar siúl aige?' rather than 'Céard atá ar siúl aige?'.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -adh/-eadh
rulesUlster.statement: Most one-syllable (first conjugation) verbs form the verbal noun by adding -adh after a broad ending and -eadh after a slender ending: dún, dúnadh; glan, glanadh; bris, briseadh; scaip, scaipeadh.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -t
rulesUlster.statement: Verbs ending in a slender consonant such as -n, -l or -r add -t to form the verbal noun: bain, baint; tiomáin, tiomáint; oscail, oscailt; freagair, freagairt; imir, imirt.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -ú/-iú
rulesUlster.statement: Most second conjugation verbs in -aigh or -igh drop that ending and take -ú (broad) or -iú (slender): gortaigh, gortú; ceartaigh, ceartú; cruinnigh, cruinniú; bailigh, bailiú.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, -ach/-each
rulesUlster.statement: A small group of -aigh/-igh verbs take -ach or -each instead of -ú/-iú: ceannaigh, ceannach; réitigh, réiteach; cuardaigh, cuardach; fuadaigh, fuadach; clúdaigh, clúdach.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, leathnú an chonsain deiridh
rulesUlster.statement: Some verbs form the verbal noun by broadening the final consonant, with no ending added: cuir, cur; siúil, siúl; iompair, iompar; ceangail, ceangal; freastail, freastal.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, briathra neamhrialta
rulesUlster.statement: The irregular verbs have their own verbal nouns which must be learned: abair, rá; beir, breith; bí, bheith; feic, feiceáil; ith, ithe; faigh, fáil; tar, teacht; téigh, dul; clois, cloisteáil; tabhair, tabhairt; déan, déanamh. In Ulster the verb 'cluin' (verbal noun cluinstin) is commonly used for 'clois', and 'tchí mé' is the present tense of 'feic', but the verbal noun stays 'feiceáil'. (Déan, déanamh is not listed in the book's table but appears in exercises B and F.)

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha, slite éagsúla eile
rulesUlster.statement: Other verbs form the verbal noun in various individual ways (-áil, -eacht, -amh, -ean, -int, -í, -ím, -íocht): nigh, ní; fág, fágáil; éirigh, éirí; lig, ligean; imigh, imeacht; cónaigh, cónaí; caith, caitheamh; seas, seasamh; dúisigh, dúiseacht; léigh, léamh; rothaigh, rothaíocht; tit, titim; inis, insint. The book's 'féach, féachaint' is replaced in Ulster by 'amharc, amharc' (ag amharc ar), a verb whose verbal noun does not change.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha gan athrú
rulesUlster.statement: Some verbs do not change at all: the verbal noun is the same as the root, including most verbs in -áil (cniotáil, bácáil, sábháil, spáráil, tástáil, pacáil, iarnáil) and others such as díol, goid, fás, léim, rith, snámh, scríobh, troid, úsáid, obair, foghlaim, stad, gáire, ól, and in Ulster amharc.

rulesUlster.point: bí leis an ainm briathartha (an aimsir láithreach agus an aimsir ghnáthláithreach)
rulesUlster.statement: The verb 'bí' is very often used with the verbal noun, for example Bíonn sé ag obair go crua. In Ulster the present forms are tá mé, tá tú, tá sé/sí, tá muid, tá sibh, tá siad (negative níl mé, níl muid; question an bhfuil mé, an bhfuil muid) and the habitual present forms are bím, bíonn tú, bíonn sé/sí, bíonn muid, bíonn sibh, bíonn siad (negative ní bhím, ní bhíonn muid; question an mbím, an mbíonn muid). The first person singular keeps its own ending (bím). The impersonal forms táthar, níltear, bítear, ní bhítear are as in the standard.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha agus an tuiseal ginideach
rulesUlster.statement: Implicit in exercise B: when 'ag' plus verbal noun is followed by a definite noun object, that noun goes into the genitive: ag gearradh an aráin, ag baint an fhéir, ag glanadh an tí, ag oscailt an dorais, ag déanamh a dhíchill.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha le 'le' agus 'ar'
rulesUlster.statement: Implicit in exercise C: 'le' plus verbal noun plus 'ag' expresses something still to be done (litir le scríobh agat, obair le déanamh agam go fóill), and 'ar' plus verbal noun gives a state (tine ar lasadh, leabhair ar díol). Ulster says 'go fóill' where the book says 'fós'.

rulesUlster.point: an t-ainm briathartha le 'a' agus séimhiú (rud a dhéanamh)
rulesUlster.statement: Implicit in exercise F: when the object comes before the verbal noun, the particle 'a' is placed between them and lenites the verbal noun: dinnéar a dhéanamh, geansaí a chniotáil, an leabhar a léamh, an fhuinneog a oscailt.

paradigmsUlster.title: A. -adh/-eadh
B. -t
C. -ú/-iú
D. -ach/-each
E. Leathnú (consan deiridh)
F. Briathra Neamhrialta
G. Slite éagsúla eile

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, a cumadh
rulesUlster.statement: The verbal adjective is formed by adding one of the endings -ta, -te, -tha, -the, -a, -e or -fa to the root (stem) of the verb. This is the only rule the book states in words; the choice of ending is taught through the exercise headings that follow. Ulster forms the verbal adjective exactly as the standard does.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -ta
rulesUlster.statement: Broad roots ending in l, n, s, ch and similar sounds take -ta: dall becomes dallta, dún becomes dúnta, múch becomes múchta. The book prints the heading as -tá, which is a misprint for -ta.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -te
rulesUlster.statement: Slender roots take -te: bris becomes briste, mill becomes millte, roinn becomes roinnte. A root ending in slender -igh drops the -igh before -te: léigh becomes léite, pléigh becomes pléite, suigh becomes suite.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -tha
rulesUlster.statement: Broad roots ending in b, c, d, g, m, p or r take -tha: cíor becomes cíortha, crom becomes cromtha, fág becomes fágtha, scuab becomes scuabtha, leag becomes leagtha.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, na foircinn -aithe agus -ithe
rulesUlster.statement: Second-conjugation verbs ending in -aigh or -igh replace that ending with -aithe (broad) or -ithe (slender): críochnaigh becomes críochnaithe, ceannaigh becomes ceannaithe, deisigh becomes deisithe, imigh becomes imithe.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -fa
rulesUlster.statement: Roots ending in -bh or -mh replace that ending with -fa: scríobh becomes scríofa, treabh becomes treafa, lobh becomes lofa.

rulesUlster.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha le tá agus ag
rulesUlster.statement: The verbal adjective is used with tá to describe a completed state (Tá an doras dúnta), and with ag plus a pronoun to say who has done the action (Tá an féar bainte agam). The book shows this through its model sentences rather than stating it. In Ulster the same pattern is used; where a noun follows ag and the article, lenite it: Tá an pháirc treafa ag an fheirmeoir.

paradigmsUlster.title: Foircinn na haidiachta briathartha
Samplaí: fréamh agus aidiacht bhriathartha
Sampla: -aithe, -ithe
forms: críochnaigh: críochnaithe (An bhfuil an obair críochnaithe agat?)

sentences.fresh: Cad chuige nach bhfuil do dhialann obair bhaile clúdaithe?
sentences.stem: Cad chuige nach bhfuil do dhialann obair bhaile (clúdaigh)?
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -aithe
sentences.note: Ulster cad chuige for cén fáth. Fresh sentence uses dialann obair bhaile from the app's school list.

sentences.ulster: Tá an pictiúr greamaithe den leabhar.
sentences.fresh: Tá an grianghraf greamaithe den chlár fógraí.
sentences.stem: Tá an grianghraf (greamaigh) den chlár fógraí.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -aithe
sentences.note: Unchanged in Ulster. Fresh sentence uses grianghraf and clár fógraí from the app's lists.

sentences.original: Bhí mé (maslaigh) nuair a dúirt sé sin.
sentences.ulster: Bhí mé maslaithe nuair a dúirt sé sin.
sentences.fresh: Bhí sí maslaithe nuair a léigh sí an teachtaireacht.
sentences.stem: Bhí sí (maslaigh) nuair a léigh sí an teachtaireacht.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -aithe
sentences.note: Unchanged in Ulster. Fresh sentence moves the insult to a message on a phone.

sentences.ulster: Níl an gluaisteán deisithe go fóill.
sentences.fresh: Níl an rothar deisithe go fóill.
sentences.stem: Níl an rothar (deisigh) go fóill.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -ithe
sentences.note: Kept gluaisteán as printed, though Ulster pupils would more often say carr; the principal may prefer carr here. Fresh sentence uses rothar from the app's transport list.

sentences.original: Tá na buachaillí (imigh) go dtí an pháirc.
sentences.ulster: Tá na buachaillí imithe go dtí an pháirc.
sentences.fresh: Tá na girseacha imithe chuig an chluiche camógaíochta.
sentences.stem: Tá na girseacha (imigh) chuig an chluiche camógaíochta.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -ithe
sentences.note: Kept buachaillí, which is used in Ulster beside gasúir. Fresh sentence uses Ulster girseacha and lenition after chuig an; please confirm the plural girseacha and the phrase chuig an chluiche.

sentences.original: Níl an leabhar (foilsigh) ach le cúpla seachtain.
sentences.ulster: Níl an leabhar foilsithe ach le cúpla seachtain.
sentences.fresh: Níl an aip foilsithe ach le cúpla lá.
sentences.stem: Níl an aip (foilsigh) ach le cúpla lá.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -ithe
sentences.note: Unchanged in Ulster. Fresh sentence moves from a book to an app released a few days ago.

sentences.ulster: An bhfuil an leabhar sínithe agat?
sentences.fresh: An bhfuil an fhoirm sínithe ag do thuismitheoirí?
sentences.stem: An bhfuil an fhoirm (sínigh) ag do thuismitheoirí?
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -ithe
sentences.note: Unchanged in Ulster. Fresh sentence is a school permission form signed by parents.

sentences.ulster: Níl an ceacht scríofa agam.
sentences.fresh: Níl an aiste scríofa agam go fóill.
sentences.stem: Níl an aiste (scríobh) agam go fóill.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -fa
sentences.note: Unchanged in Ulster. Fresh sentence adds go fóill.

sentences.original: Tá an pháirc (treabh) ag an bhfeirmeoir.
sentences.ulster: Tá an pháirc treafa ag an fheirmeoir.
sentences.fresh: Tá an talamh treafa ag an fheirmeoir cheana féin.
sentences.stem: Tá an talamh (treabh) ag an fheirmeoir cheana féin.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -fa
sentences.note: Ulster lenites after ag an: ag an fheirmeoir, not ag an bhfeirmeoir. Fresh sentence keeps the same construction.

sentences.ulster: Tá na prátaí lofa.
sentences.fresh: Tá na húlla lofa sa mhála.
sentences.stem: Tá na húlla (lobh) sa mhála.
sentences.point: an aidiacht bhriathartha, an foirceann -fa
sentences.note: Unchanged in Ulster. Fresh sentence uses mála from the app's list; sa mhála is the same in Ulster and the standard.
